question: Many representation-theoretic results for finite groups (invariant complements, complete reducibility, character orthogonality) are proved using the averaging (1/|G|) sum_{g in G}. For compact groups this is replaced by integration against the Haar probability measure. Delineate carefully which statements carry over verbatim to infinite compact groups and which must be modified or fail. In particular address: (a) existence of invariant complements and complete reducibility; (b) finite-dimensionality of irreducible representations; (c) the identity sum_i (dim W_i)^2 = |G| and formulas explicitly involving |G|.
reference_answer: The key replacement is: the normalized finite average (1/|G|) sum_g, which is an invariant probability measure on a finite group, becomes the Haar integral integral_G . dg against the unique invariant probability measure dg guaranteed for any compact group (invariant under left and right translation, normalized so integral_G 1 dg = 1). Wherever a proof used only the invariance and normalization of the average, it carries over verbatim with sum replaced by integral. (a) Invariant complements and complete reducibility DO carry over: the Weyl unitarity trick defines <v|w>_G = integral_G <phi(g)v | phi(g)w> dg, which is still a well-defined G-invariant inner product (the integrand is continuous and the measure finite), making phi unitary and giving every invariant subspace an invariant complement; thus every finite-dimensional representation over C of a compact group is completely reducible - verbatim analogue of Maschke. (b) Finite-dimensionality of irreducibles: for FINITE groups every irrep is automatically finite-dimensional (it is a subrepresentation of the finite-dimensional regular representation). For infinite compact groups one must RESTRICT attention or prove a theorem: it is a nontrivial theorem (Peter-Weyl) that every irreducible UNITARY representation of a compact group is finite-dimensional; this does not come for free from averaging and is a genuine modification of the finite-group situation (where it was trivial). (c) Formulas with |G| must be modified or fail: the identity sum_i (dim W_i)^2 = |G| and 'multiplicity of W_i in the regular representation equals dim W_i summing to |G|' involve the finite cardinality |G|, which is infinite for an infinite compact group. The regular representation becomes L^2(G), which is infinite-dimensional when G is infinite; the correct compact-group statement is that L^2(G) decomposes as a Hilbert-space direct sum of all irreducible unitary representations, each with multiplicity equal to its dimension (Peter-Weyl), and the matrix coefficients form an orthonormal basis - but any expression literally equal to |G| is no longer valid. Character orthogonality (chi_i, chi_j) = delta_{ij} survives with the inner product (x,y) = integral_G conj(x(g)) y(g) dg, since it too used only invariance/normalization; however the counting statement 'number of irreps = number of conjugacy classes' and sums over the finite group do not transfer. Summary: averaging-based existence results (invariant complements, complete reducibility, character orthonormality) carry over by replacing sum with the Haar integral; statements relying on the finiteness of |G| (the dimension-squared sum, finite-dimensional regular representation) fail and are replaced by Peter-Weyl, and finite-dimensionality of irreducibles becomes a theorem rather than an automatic fact.

question: For a finite-dimensional representation (phi, V) of a group G, the dual representation (phi^*, V^*) is defined by phi^*(g)(L) = L . phi(g)^{-1}. (a) Prove that in a basis phi^*(g) = phi(g^{-1})^T, and that if (phi, V) is unitary then phi^*(g) = conj(phi(g)) (the entrywise complex conjugate). (b) Delineate the boundary between a representation and its dual: give the character relation chi_{V^*}(g) = conj(chi_V(g)) for unitary representations, and explain precisely when V is isomorphic to its dual (self-dual) versus not, giving an explicit example of a NON-self-dual irreducible representation. (c) State what remains true regardless: (phi^*, V^*) is irreducible iff (phi, V) is.
reference_answer: (a) By definition phi^*(g)(L) = L . phi(g)^{-1} for L in V^*. Fixing dual bases, the matrix of the map L -> L . phi(g)^{-1} acting on row vectors is right multiplication by phi(g)^{-1}, which on column-vector (coordinate) representation of V^* is the transpose: phi^*(g) = (phi(g)^{-1})^T = phi(g^{-1})^T, using phi(g)^{-1} = phi(g^{-1}). If (phi, V) is unitary, then phi(g)^{-1} = phi(g)^dagger = conj(phi(g))^T, so phi(g^{-1})^T = (phi(g)^dagger)^T = (conj(phi(g))^T)^T = conj(phi(g)); hence phi^*(g) = conj(phi(g)), the entrywise complex conjugate. (b) Taking traces of the character: chi_{V^*}(g) = tr(phi^*(g)) = tr(phi(g^{-1})^T) = tr(phi(g^{-1})) = chi_V(g^{-1}); for unitary phi this equals conj(chi_V(g)) because chi_V(g^{-1}) = conj(chi_V(g)) for unitary representations (eigenvalues of phi(g) lie on the unit circle, so inverse = conjugate). Thus chi_{V^*}(g) = conj(chi_V(g)). The boundary: V is self-dual (V ~ V^*) iff chi_V = chi_{V^*}, i.e. iff chi_V(g) = conj(chi_V(g)) for all g, i.e. iff the character is real-valued. So real-character (in particular all-real-matrix, e.g. permutation) representations are self-dual, while a representation with a genuinely complex character is NOT self-dual. Explicit non-self-dual example: let G = Z/3 = <g> and let (phi, C) be the one-dimensional irrep phi(g) = omega, where omega = e^{2 pi i/3} is a primitive cube root of unity. Its character is chi(g) = omega, which is not real (omega != conj(omega) = omega^2). Its dual is phi^*(g) = conj(omega) = omega^2, the OTHER nontrivial irrep of Z/3; since omega != omega^2, phi and phi^* have different characters and are inequivalent, so this irrep is not self-dual. (c) Regardless of self-duality, (phi^*, V^*) is irreducible iff (phi, V) is: invariant subspaces of V^* correspond (via annihilators) bijectively and inclusion-reversingly to invariant subspaces of V, so V^* has only the trivial invariant subspaces iff V does. question: A POVM P = {P_i : i in [2^m]} is implemented through block encodings as follows. For each outcome i we are given a unitary U_i that is a (beta, a)-block-encoding of sqrt(P_i), all sharing the SAME ancilla size a and the SAME subnormalization factor beta > 0, so that U_i |0^a> |psi> = (1/beta) |0^a> sqrt(P_i) |psi> + |perp_i>, where (<0^a| tensor I)|perp_i> = 0. Define the controlled unitary W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i acting on an output register in the uniform superposition |u> = (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i |i>, an ancilla register |0^a>, and the system register |psi>. After applying W one measures the ancilla register and postselects on the outcome 0^a. Starting from |u> |0^a> |psi>, derive in full the probability P(succ) of obtaining 0^a on the ancilla, show that it equals exactly 1/(beta^2 2^m) independent of the input state |psi>, and identify precisely where the POVM completeness relation sum_i P_i = I and the mutual orthogonality of the output-register basis states are used.
reference_answer: Apply W to the uniform-superposition input. Because W is block-diagonal in the output register, W |u> |0^a> |psi> = (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i |i> (U_i |0^a> |psi>) = (1/(beta sqrt(2^m))) sum_i |i> |0^a> sqrt(P_i)|psi> + |perp>, where |perp> = (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i |i> |perp_i> satisfies (I tensor <0^a| tensor I)|perp> = 0 because each (<0^a| tensor I)|perp_i> = 0. Postselecting the ancilla on 0^a projects out |perp> entirely, since |perp> has zero overlap with the subspace spanned by |0^a> on the ancilla. The unnormalized postselected vector is therefore (1/(beta sqrt(2^m))) sum_i |i> |0^a> sqrt(P_i)|psi>. Its squared norm is the success probability. The output-register states |i> are mutually orthonormal, so the cross terms vanish and the norm squared factorizes outcome by outcome: P(succ) = (1/(beta^2 2^m)) sum_i || sqrt(P_i)|psi> ||^2 = (1/(beta^2 2^m)) sum_i <psi| sqrt(P_i)^dagger sqrt(P_i) |psi> = (1/(beta^2 2^m)) sum_i <psi| P_i |psi>. Here we used sqrt(P_i)^dagger sqrt(P_i) = P_i because each P_i is positive semidefinite and sqrt(P_i) is its unique PSD square root. Finally, by POVM completeness sum_i P_i = I, so sum_i <psi| P_i |psi> = <psi| I |psi> = 1 for any normalized |psi>. Hence P(succ) = 1/(beta^2 2^m), which is manifestly independent of |psi>. Completeness is what collapses the state-dependent sum to the constant 1; the orthogonality of the |i> is what prevents interference between different outcomes so the sum of norms (not a norm of a sum) appears.

question: In the block-encoding implementation of a 2^m-outcome POVM via W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i (each U_i a (beta,a)-block-encoding of sqrt(P_i)), a single run succeeds (ancilla returns 0^a) with probability P(succ) = 1/(beta^2 2^m). Explain quantitatively why naive repetition is wasteful, and show that amplitude amplification raises the success probability to a constant while using only O(beta 2^{m/2} log(1/delta)) queries to W and W^dagger to reach failure probability at most delta. State clearly which quantity plays the role of the 'good' amplitude, why the amplification cost scales as 1/sqrt(P(succ)), and where the logarithmic factor log(1/delta) comes from.
reference_answer: Naive repetition: a single run flags success with probability p := P(succ) = 1/(beta^2 2^m), so the expected number of independent repetitions to see one success is 1/p = beta^2 2^m, which grows exponentially in m. Each repetition uses O(1) queries to W, so naive repetition costs O(beta^2 2^m) queries. Amplitude amplification: the postselected run prepares a state of the form sqrt(p) |good> + sqrt(1-p) |bad>, where |good> is the normalized component with the ancilla equal to 0^a (the 'good' amplitude is sqrt(p)). Standard amplitude amplification applies O(1/sqrt(p)) rounds, each round being one call to the preparation unitary (built from W) and its inverse (hence W^dagger), interleaved with reflections about |good> and about the initial state. After O(1/sqrt(p)) = O(beta 2^{m/2}) rounds the amplitude of |good> is rotated to Theta(1), so a single final measurement succeeds with constant probability. The quadratic speedup is exactly the replacement of 1/p (classical) by 1/sqrt(p) (quantum): amplitude amplification rotates an angle theta with sin^2(theta) = p by equal increments, and reaching angle pi/2 needs O(1/theta) = O(1/sqrt(p)) steps since theta ~ sqrt(p) for small p. The log(1/delta) factor: one amplified round still leaves a constant failure probability c < 1; to drive the total failure probability below delta one repeats the amplified procedure O(log(1/delta)) times (majority/until-success), each repetition independently failing with probability at most c, so c^{O(log(1/delta))} <= delta. Multiplying the per-amplification cost O(beta 2^{m/2}) by the O(log(1/delta)) outer repetitions gives the total query count O(beta 2^{m/2} log(1/delta)) to W and W^dagger.

question: Two normalized but possibly non-orthogonal pure states |psi> and |phi> are given with overlap c := <psi|phi>, |c| < 1, and we are promised the unknown state is one of them. Consider the three-element POVM with P_psi = (1/(1+|c|)) |phi_perp><phi_perp|, P_phi = (1/(1+|c|)) |psi_perp><psi_perp|, and P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi, where |psi_perp> := (|phi> - c|psi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) and |phi_perp> := (|psi> - c*|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2). Demonstrate by a concrete counterexample-style argument that NO two-element POVM {E_psi, E_phi} (with only the two conclusive labels and no inconclusive outcome) can be unambiguous, i.e. cannot simultaneously satisfy <phi|E_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|E_phi|psi> = 0 while being a valid POVM, whenever 0 < |c| < 1. Then verify that the given three-element POVM is unambiguous and explain why introducing P_? is exactly the structural escape that restores validity.
reference_answer: Unambiguity requires E_psi to never fire on phi and E_phi to never fire on psi: <phi|E_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|E_phi|psi> = 0. Since E_psi, E_phi are PSD, <phi|E_psi|phi> = 0 forces E_psi|phi> = 0 (a PSD operator with zero expectation on a vector annihilates it), so range(E_psi) is orthogonal to |phi>; in the two-dimensional span{|psi>,|phi>} this means E_psi is supported on the one-dimensional complement of |phi>, i.e. E_psi = a |phi_perp><phi_perp| for some a >= 0. Likewise E_phi = b |psi_perp><psi_perp|, b >= 0. A two-element POVM must satisfy completeness E_psi + E_phi = I on span{|psi>,|phi>}. Take the matrix element in state |psi>: <psi|E_psi|psi> + <psi|E_phi|psi> = <psi|I|psi> = 1. But <psi|E_phi|psi> = 0 by unambiguity, so <psi|E_psi|psi> = 1. Now <psi|E_psi|psi> = a |<psi|phi_perp>|^2. Compute <psi|phi_perp> = (<psi|psi> - c<psi|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = (1 - |c|^2)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = sqrt(1-|c|^2). So a (1-|c|^2) = 1, giving a = 1/(1-|c|^2). By symmetry b = 1/(1-|c|^2). Then E_psi + E_phi = (1/(1-|c|^2)) (|phi_perp><phi_perp| + |psi_perp><psi_perp|). This operator does NOT equal I when c != 0: its trace is 2/(1-|c|^2) > 2 = Tr(I on the 2D space) whenever |c| > 0, so E_psi + E_phi != I. Hence no valid two-element unambiguous POVM exists for 0 < |c| < 1 -- completeness is violated because the two rank-one effects are forced to be too 'heavy'. The fix: keep P_psi, P_phi rank-one on |phi_perp>, |psi_perp> but SHRINK their weights to 1/(1+|c|) (instead of the forced 1/(1-|c|^2) = 1/((1-|c|)(1+|c|))), and absorb the deficit into P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi. One checks P_psi, P_phi >= 0 trivially, and P_? >= 0 because the weight 1/(1+|c|) is small enough (the eigenvalues of P_psi+P_phi on the 2D space are (1 +/- |c|)/(1+|c|), so its operator norm is exactly 1 and I - (P_psi+P_phi) >= 0). Unambiguity still holds: <phi|P_psi|phi> ∝ |<phi|phi_perp>|^2 = 0 and <psi|P_phi|psi> ∝ |<psi|psi_perp>|^2 = 0. Thus the inconclusive outcome P_? is not cosmetic: it is the exact slack that lets positivity and completeness coexist with unambiguity once the states overlap.

question: For the unambiguous-discrimination POVM with P_psi = (1/(1+|c|)) |phi_perp><phi_perp|, P_phi = (1/(1+|c|)) |psi_perp><psi_perp|, P_? = I - P_psi - P_phi, where c = <psi|phi>, |c| < 1, and |psi_perp>, |phi_perp> are defined as in the text, prove the three properties that make it a legitimate unambiguous POVM for state discrimination: (i) P_psi, P_phi, P_? are all positive semidefinite; (ii) P_psi + P_phi + P_? = I; (iii) the conclusive outcomes are unambiguous, i.e. <phi|P_psi|phi> = 0 and <psi|P_phi|psi> = 0. For (i) you must actually verify that P_? >= 0, not merely assert it, by diagonalizing I - P_psi - P_phi on the two-dimensional space span{|psi>,|phi>}.
reference_answer: Property (ii) is immediate from the definition P_? := I - P_psi - P_phi, so P_psi + P_phi + P_? = I exactly, with no assumption on c. Property (iii): compute <phi|phi_perp>. Since |phi_perp> = (|psi> - c*|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2), we get <phi|phi_perp> = (<phi|psi> - c*<phi|phi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = (c* - c*)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = 0 (using <phi|psi> = c* and <phi|phi>=1). Hence <phi|P_psi|phi> = (1/(1+|c|))|<phi|phi_perp>|^2 = 0. Symmetrically, <psi|psi_perp> = (<psi|phi> - c<psi|psi>)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = (c - c)/sqrt(1-|c|^2) = 0, so <psi|P_phi|psi> = 0. The conclusive outcomes never fire on the wrong state. Property (i): P_psi, P_phi are nonnegative multiples of rank-one projectors |phi_perp><phi_perp|, |psi_perp><psi_perp|, hence PSD. For P_?, restrict to span{|psi>,|phi>} (off this plane I - P_psi - P_phi acts as the identity, which is PSD). Both |phi_perp> and |psi_perp> are unit vectors; a direct computation of their overlap gives |<phi_perp|psi_perp>| = |c|. In the (non-orthogonal) spanning pair {|phi_perp>, |psi_perp>}, the operator S := P_psi + P_phi = (1/(1+|c|))(|phi_perp><phi_perp| + |psi_perp><psi_perp|) is a scaled sum of two unit rank-one projectors with Gram overlap |c|; such a sum has eigenvalues (1 +/- |c|) times the scalar 1/(1+|c|), i.e. eigenvalues 1 and (1-|c|)/(1+|c|). Hence ||S|| = 1 (attained) and the smaller eigenvalue is (1-|c|)/(1+|c|) >= 0. Therefore P_? = I - S has eigenvalues 1 - 1 = 0 and 1 - (1-|c|)/(1+|c|) = 2|c|/(1+|c|), both >= 0 for |c| in [0,1). So P_? >= 0 (with a zero eigenvalue, showing the weight 1/(1+|c|) is the largest that keeps P_? PSD). All three properties hold, so the family is a valid unambiguous-discrimination POVM.

question: Lemma 9.15 assumes that for every outcome i the block encoding U_i of sqrt(P_i) uses the SAME ancilla size a and the SAME subnormalization factor beta. Investigate what breaks if these two uniformity assumptions are dropped. Specifically: (a) if the U_i had different subnormalization factors beta_i, show that the controlled unitary W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i followed by postselection on 0^a would NOT yield the clean superposition sum_i |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi> that is needed, and identify what spurious operator appears instead; (b) if the U_i used different ancilla registers (different sizes a_i, or disjoint ancillas), explain why a single joint postselection event '0^a' is no longer well defined and how this changes the success-probability bookkeeping. In each case state the minimal fix (if any) that restores the construction.
reference_answer: (a) Different beta_i. The block-encoding action becomes U_i |0^a>|psi> = (1/beta_i) |0^a> sqrt(P_i)|psi> + |perp_i>. After W on the uniform superposition and postselection on 0^a, the surviving (unnormalized) joint state is (1/sqrt(2^m)) sum_i (1/beta_i) |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi>. This is NOT proportional to the required sum_i |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi>: the weights are distorted by the factors 1/beta_i. Measuring the output register then yields label i with probability proportional to (1/beta_i^2) <psi|P_i|psi> rather than <psi|P_i|psi>, i.e. the effective implemented family is {P_i' = P_i/beta_i^2} (up to normalization), a DIFFERENT and generally non-complete measurement because sum_i P_i/beta_i^2 != I in general. The spurious object is a diagonal reweighting by 1/beta_i^2; statistics are biased toward outcomes with small beta_i. Minimal fix: rescale to a common beta := max_i beta_i by replacing each U_i with a block encoding of (beta_i/beta) sqrt(P_i) (pad the subnormalization up), or equivalently prepare the output register in a NON-uniform superposition sum_i (beta_i/beta)|i> designed to cancel the 1/beta_i weights, restoring sum_i |i> sqrt(P_i)|psi> after postselection. The uniform-superposition PREP and the common beta are two sides of the same requirement. (b) Different ancillas. If U_i acts on its own ancilla register of size a_i (or on disjoint physical ancillas), then 'measure the ancilla and postselect on 0^a' is ambiguous: there is no single shared register whose value 0^a flags success for every branch simultaneously. In W = sum_i |i><i| tensor U_i, branch i touches ancilla-set i while leaving the others idle, so a global postselection onto all-zeros across the union of ancillas conflates 'U_i produced its clean block' with 'the idle ancillas of the other branches happen to read 0', double counting and breaking the clean identity (I tensor <0^a| tensor I)|perp> = 0 that was essential. The bookkeeping P(succ) = (1/(beta^2 2^m)) sum_i <psi|P_i|psi> relied on a single projector |0^a><0^a| commuting with the branch structure; with per-branch ancillas the projector factorizes differently per branch and the sum no longer collapses by completeness. Minimal fix: use one shared ancilla register of common size a = max_i a_i, embedding each U_i so that it only returns the designated register to 0^a on its clean block (pad smaller encodings with unused-but-reset ancilla qubits), which is exactly the 'same ancilla size a' hypothesis. There is no cheaper fix that avoids a shared success flag: without it the postselection event is not a single projector and the completeness collapse fails.

question: Given a real matrix A with ||A||_max < 1 and A_ij real, suppose we have a bit oracle that writes a d'-bit fixed-point representation of A_ij into a work register: O~_A |0^{d'}>|i>|j> = |A~_ij>|i>|j>. Using classical arithmetic one first produces O'_A |0^d>|i>|j> = |theta~_ij>|i>|j> with theta~_ij = arccos(A_ij)/pi in [0,1) a d-bit value. Then a controlled rotation CR transfers theta~_ij to the amplitude of a fresh ancilla qubit. Prove that the full procedure O_A = (I_1 tensor (O'_A)^{-1}) * CR * (I_1 tensor O'_A), acting on |0>|0^d>|i>|j>, produces exactly the amplitude-oracle state (A~_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) |1>) |0^d>|i>|j>, i.e. with the d-bit work register returned to |0^d>. State precisely why the final uncomputation step (O'_A)^{-1} is mandatory -- i.e. why the work register cannot simply be discarded ('no free cleanup') -- and what would go wrong with the amplitude oracle's action if it were left entangled.
reference_answer: Track the registers (ancilla qubit, d-bit work register, index registers i,j). Step 1 (apply I_1 tensor O'_A): |0>|0^d>|i>|j> -> |0>|theta~_ij>|i>|j>. The index registers are untouched; the work register now holds the angle. Step 2 (controlled rotation CR, controlled on the work register, acting on the ancilla qubit): CR implements |0>|theta~> -> (cos(pi theta~)|0> + sin(pi theta~)|1>)|theta~>. With A~_ij := cos(pi theta~_ij) (and theta~_ij = arccos(A_ij)/pi so cos(pi theta~_ij) = A_ij up to the d-bit rounding), this gives (A~_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) |1>) |theta~_ij>|i>|j>, using sin(pi theta~) = sqrt(1 - cos^2(pi theta~)) = sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) >= 0 for theta~ in [0,1) (nonnegative sine on (0,pi)). Step 3 (apply I_1 tensor (O'_A)^{-1}): the rotation acted only on the ancilla qubit and did NOT alter the work register, so (O'_A)^{-1} maps |theta~_ij>|i>|j> back to |0^d>|i>|j> conditioned on each (i,j). Crucially (O'_A)^{-1} is a function only of (i,j), which are unchanged, so it uncomputes the angle coherently and uniformly across the ancilla's |0> and |1> branches (it acts as identity on the ancilla qubit). The result is (A~_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - A~_ij^2) |1>) |0^d>|i>|j>, exactly the amplitude oracle O_A with the work register restored. Why uncomputation is mandatory (no free cleanup): if we skipped (O'_A)^{-1} and merely 'discarded' |theta~_ij>, the true quantum state is (A~_ij|0> + sqrt(1-A~_ij^2)|1>) |theta~_ij>|i>|j> -- the ancilla qubit is correlated with the work register through the shared dependence on (i,j). Tracing out (discarding) the work register leaves a MIXED state on the ancilla+index registers whenever different (i,j) produce different theta~, destroying the coherent superposition A~_ij|0> + sqrt(1-A~_ij^2)|1>. Worse, when O_A is used inside a larger block-encoding circuit that interferes different (i,j) branches (e.g. the sparse-matrix LCU of Fig. 9.7), the residual record |theta~_ij> acts as a which-path marker: branches with different angles no longer interfere, so the intended matrix element <0|<i|U_A|0>|j> = A_ij is corrupted into a decohered, generally wrong value. Hence the garbage register must be coherently returned to |0^d> by (O'_A)^{-1}; discarding is not free because a quantum computer cannot erase an entangled register without either uncomputation or decoherence. The ancilla qubit carrying the amplitude is deliberately NOT uncomputed -- it is the output -- but the intermediate angle register must be.

question: The amplitude oracle O_A |0>|i>|j> = (A_ij |0> + sqrt(1 - |A_ij|^2) |1>) |i>|j> is often introduced alongside a standing convenience assumption ||A||_max < 1. Determine the EXACT condition under which the right-hand side is a valid normalized state and the oracle is a legitimate unitary action, by analyzing the three regimes |A_ij| < 1, |A_ij| = 1, and |A_ij| > 1 (for each: is it a unit vector, what does the controlled-rotation angle do, does the oracle exist). Then state carefully whether the strict inequality ||A||_max < 1 is NECESSARY or merely a sufficient convenience, explain the downstream consequence for the subnormalization factor of the resulting block encoding, and why one preprocesses A by dividing out an upper bound on ||A||_max before building the oracle.
reference_answer: The right-hand side A_ij|0> + sqrt(1-|A_ij|^2)|1> is a unit vector with a real nonnegative second coefficient iff 1 - |A_ij|^2 >= 0, i.e. iff |A_ij| <= 1. The sharp validity condition is therefore |A_ij| <= 1, NOT the strict |A_ij| < 1. Regime |A_ij| < 1: 1 - |A_ij|^2 > 0, the state is a genuine normalized superposition with rotation angle theta = 2 arccos(|A_ij|) strictly in (0,pi); the amplitude of |0> faithfully encodes A_ij with both branches populated. Regime |A_ij| = 1: 1 - |A_ij|^2 = 0, so the second (sqrt) term is exactly zero and the state is A_ij|0> (a unit vector, basis state up to phase). This is a perfectly LEGITIMATE normalized amplitude oracle -- the rotation angle is simply 0 or pi (an endpoint of the range), and O_A remains a valid unitary action; nothing degenerates about its validity. The only caveat is purely numerical: if finite-precision arithmetic rounds A~_ij slightly ABOVE 1, then sqrt(1-A~_ij^2) becomes imaginary, so one keeps a small guard below 1 for robustness. But |A_ij| = 1 itself is inside the valid regime. Regime |A_ij| > 1: now 1 - |A_ij|^2 < 0 and sqrt(1 - |A_ij|^2) is imaginary, so there is no real controlled-rotation producing A_ij|0> + sqrt(1-|A_ij|^2)|1> as a unit vector; the amplitude oracle of this form does not exist. An entry of magnitude strictly above 1 cannot be encoded as a single-qubit amplitude. Necessity vs sufficiency: the oracle exists and is normalized for the full closed range |A_ij| <= 1, so ||A||_max <= 1 (allowing equality) is the actual requirement. The strict ||A||_max < 1 commonly assumed in the text is a SUFFICIENT CONVENIENCE, not a necessity: it guarantees a non-degenerate two-branch rotation for every entry and a numerical margin against rounding above 1, but entries exactly equal to 1 are still fine. It is only |A_ij| > 1 that is genuinely excluded. Downstream: a block encoding built from the oracle has subnormalization factor at least ||A|| (for the s-sparse LCU construction exactly alpha = s ||A||_max). If some |A_ij| > 1 the per-entry amplitude encoding is impossible; and even in the valid regime a larger ||A||_max pushes alpha up. Therefore one preprocesses by choosing a known upper bound M >= ||A||_max and building the oracle for A/M, whose entries satisfy |(A/M)_ij| <= 1, guaranteeing valid normalized states and a controlled subnormalization; taking M strictly above ||A||_max additionally restores the strict-inequality numerical margin.

question: Two input models for the entries of a matrix A appear in the sparse block-encoding discussion: the BIT oracle O~_A |0^{d'}>|i>|j> = |A~_ij>|i>|j>, which writes a classical fixed-point string into a register, and the AMPLITUDE oracle O_A |0>|i>|j> = (A_ij|0> + sqrt(1-|A_ij|^2)|1>)|i>|j>, which encodes the entry as the amplitude of an ancilla qubit. Explain conceptually (i) what distinguishes the two as computational resources -- which is a 'digital/query' interface and which is an 'analog/amplitude' interface; (ii) why building the amplitude oracle from the bit oracle requires both controlled rotations (gate work) and uncomputation (query work), i.e. the amplitude oracle is strictly derived, not primitive; and (iii) in a resource count for the overall block encoding, why it is natural to charge the construction one forward and one inverse bit-oracle query plus the gates of a controlled rotation, and why the work register must be counted as borrowed (returned clean), not consumed.
reference_answer: (i) The bit oracle is a DIGITAL/query interface: it deposits a classical bit string A~_ij into a register, which can be read, fanned out via CNOTs, and processed by reversible arithmetic. It makes the numeric value explicitly available but says nothing by itself about amplitudes. The amplitude oracle is an ANALOG/amplitude interface: it hides the value A_ij in the probability amplitude of |0> on an ancilla qubit, which is exactly the form a block encoding needs (the encoded entry must appear as an <0|...|0>-type amplitude), but which cannot be read out directly without measurement/estimation. The two interfaces trade explicitness (bit) for direct usability inside interference-based circuits (amplitude). (ii) The amplitude oracle is derived, not primitive: to turn a stored value into an amplitude one must (a) convert A~_ij to an angle theta~_ij via reversible classical arithmetic (a bit-oracle-type query O'_A), (b) perform a controlled Y-rotation CR that maps the angle into the ancilla amplitude -- irreducibly gate work, since no bit oracle produces amplitudes on its own -- and (c) uncompute the angle register with (O'_A)^{-1}, a second (inverse) query, to disentangle the amplitude qubit from the intermediate data. Thus amplitude oracle = query + controlled-rotation gates + inverse query. The rotation is where 'digital' becomes 'analog'; the two queries bracket it to keep the transformation reversible. (iii) Resource accounting: the natural charge is one forward bit-oracle query O'_A, the controlled-rotation gate(s) CR (whose gate count grows with the angle precision d), and one inverse query (O'_A)^{-1}. Both the forward and inverse queries are counted because reversibility forces the uncomputation; you cannot amortize it away. The d-bit work register is counted as BORROWED/clean ancilla: it starts in |0^d> and must be returned to |0^d> by the uncomputation, so it does not add to the persistent ancilla budget of the block encoding (it is reusable across calls), but it is NOT free either -- it must physically exist during the call and the inverse query must be paid for. Counting it as consumed would overstate the ancilla footprint; counting the uncomputation as free would understate the query/gate cost. The honest ledger is: +2 queries, +CR gates, +d borrowed-and-returned work qubits, +1 persistent amplitude ancilla (the actual output qubit), with 'no free cleanup' meaning the inverse query is a real line item.

question: Let A be a diagonal N x N matrix (a 1-sparse matrix whose only nonzero entries are A_ii), with ||A||_max <= 1. Using the simplified amplitude oracle O_A |0>|i> = (A_ii |0> + sqrt(1 - |A_ii|^2) |1>) |i>, set U_A := O_A. Prove by direct evaluation of the matrix element <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> that U_A is a (1,1)-block-encoding of A, i.e. <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> = A_ii delta_ij, so THIS construction has subnormalization factor alpha = 1 with a single ancilla qubit. Explain why no index-permutation oracle is needed here, in contrast to the general 1-sparse case. Then discuss precisely in what sense alpha = 1 is or is not optimal: state the general lower bound any block encoding must obey, and say whether alpha = 1 is a global optimum for every diagonal A with ||A||_max <= 1 or only in a specific case.
reference_answer: Apply U_A = O_A to |0>|j>: U_A |0>|j> = (A_jj |0> + sqrt(1-|A_jj|^2)|1>)|j>. Now take the overlap with <0|<i|: <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> = A_jj <0|0> <i|j> + sqrt(1-|A_jj|^2) <0|1> <i|j>. The second term vanishes because <0|1> = 0. The first term is A_jj <i|j> = A_jj delta_ij. When i = j this equals A_jj = A_ii; when i != j it is 0. Hence <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> = A_ii delta_ij, which is precisely the (i,j) entry of the diagonal matrix A. By the definition of block encoding, (<0| tensor I) U_A (|0> tensor I) = A exactly, with one ancilla qubit (m = 1) and subnormalization alpha = 1, so U_A is in BE_{1,1}(A). No permutation oracle is needed because for a DIAGONAL matrix the row index equals the column index: the single nonzero entry in column j sits at row c(j) = j, i.e. the sparsity permutation c is the identity. In the general 1-sparse case the unique nonzero entry of column j lives at row c(j) != j, so one must apply an index permutation O_c |j> = |c(j)> to move the amplitude-carrying basis state from |j> to |c(j)>; for the diagonal case c = id, so O_c = I and U_A = O_A alone suffices. Optimality -- stated carefully. The general lower bound is that any (alpha,m)-block-encoding of A must satisfy alpha >= ||A|| (operator norm), because the encoded top-left block equals A/alpha and a sub-block of a unitary has operator norm at most 1, forcing ||A||/alpha <= 1. For a diagonal A, ||A|| = max_i |A_ii|. The present construction FIXES alpha = 1 regardless of the entries; this value saturates the lower bound (hence is globally optimal) ONLY in the case ||A|| = max_i |A_ii| = 1, e.g. when some |A_ii| = 1. If instead max_i |A_ii| = r < 1 strictly, then alpha = 1 is a VALID but NOT optimal subnormalization: the lower bound only demands alpha >= r, and a smaller alpha = r is mathematically achievable -- for example by encoding A/r (whose max entry has modulus 1) with this very construction to obtain an (r,1)-block-encoding of A. Thus alpha = 1 is a property of THIS fixed construction, globally optimal exactly when ||A|| = 1, and for ||A|| < 1 merely a valid upper bound rather than the minimum. The honest statement: the construction yields alpha = 1; it meets the alpha >= ||A|| floor iff ||A|| = 1, and is not subnormalization-optimal when ||A|| < 1.

question: To block-encode a general s-sparse matrix A (at most s nonzeros per row and per column, ||A||_max = 1), one decomposes A into 1-sparse pieces. View the sparsity pattern as a bipartite graph with left vertices the row indices and right vertices the column indices, with an edge (i,j) whenever A_ij != 0; pad with zero entries so every row and column has exactly s incident edges, making the graph s-regular. Prove that this s-regular bipartite graph decomposes into exactly s disjoint perfect matchings, so that A = sum_{ell in [s]} A^{(ell)} with each A^{(ell)} 1-sparse, and explain how each matching ell yields a permutation j -> c(j,ell) of [N] that can be queried by a single permutation oracle O_c |ell>|j> = |ell>|c(j,ell)>. Then explain why this is precisely what makes the LCU circuit of Fig. 9.7 produce a block encoding with subnormalization factor alpha = s, and why alpha = s (= s ||A||_max) is the natural choice rather than something smaller.
reference_answer: Edge decomposition: an s-regular bipartite graph has, by Koenig's line-coloring theorem (edge-coloring version), chromatic index exactly s, i.e. its edges can be properly colored with s colors so that no two edges of the same color share a vertex. Each color class is therefore a set of vertex-disjoint edges covering -- because the graph is s-regular and bipartite with equal side sizes N -- every vertex exactly once; that is a PERFECT MATCHING. There are exactly s color classes, so the edge set partitions into s disjoint perfect matchings M_1,...,M_s. From matchings to permutations: fix matching ell. In a perfect matching every column vertex j is matched to a unique row vertex, call it c(j,ell); conversely every row is matched to a unique column. Hence j -> c(j,ell) is a bijection of [N] onto itself, i.e. a permutation. Packaging all s matchings, the single oracle O_c |ell>|j> = |ell>|c(j,ell)> encodes, for each color ell, the corresponding permutation. 1-sparse pieces: define A^{(ell)} by A^{(ell)}_{c(j,ell),j} = A_{c(j,ell),j} and all other entries zero. Each A^{(ell)} has exactly one nonzero per row and per column (it is supported on matching M_ell), so it is 1-sparse; and because the s matchings partition ALL edges of the (padded) graph, every nonzero entry A_ij belongs to exactly one matching, giving A = sum_{ell in [s]} A^{(ell)}. LCU and alpha = s: the circuit uses the s-qubit Hadamard-type map D |0^s> = (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell |ell> to form a uniform superposition over the s matchings, O_A to load the entry amplitude for the selected matching, and O_c to route the index; this is an LCU over the equal-weight family {A^{(ell)}} with s terms each of 1-norm (coefficient) at most ||A||_max = 1. The standard LCU block-encoding subnormalization is the coefficient 1-norm, here sum_ell 1 = s. So U_A in BE_{s, s+1}(A), i.e. <0|<0^s|<i| U_A |0>|0^s>|j> = (1/s) A_ij, matching alpha = s. Why alpha = s is natural: Lemma 2.46 gives ||A|| <= s ||A||_max, and any block encoding must satisfy alpha >= ||A||, which for a worst-case s-sparse matrix can be as large as s ||A||_max; the construction attains alpha = s ||A||_max = s, so it meets the generic sparse bound. One cannot generally pick alpha < s with this oracle structure because the equal 1/sqrt(s) amplitudes spread the single real entry over s branches, giving exactly a 1/s matrix element; a smaller alpha would require either knowing the entries are smaller (reducing ||A||_max) or using a non-uniform PREP tailored to the actual row/column norms.

question: Consider the s-sparse LCU block-encoding circuit U_A = (I tensor D tensor I)(I tensor O_c) O_A (I tensor D tensor I), where D |0^s> = (1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell in [s]} |ell>, O_A |0>|ell>|j> = (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1 - |A_{c(j,ell),j}|^2)|1>)|ell>|j>, and O_c |ell>|j> = |ell>|c(j,ell)>, with each j -> c(j,ell) a permutation. By propagating |0>|0^s>|j> through D, O_A, O_c and separately propagating |0>|0^s>|i> through D (using that D is Hermitian), evaluate the inner product <0|<0^s|<i| U_A |0>|0^s>|j> and show it equals (1/s) A_ij. Explain carefully why the single clean sum over ell collapses to one surviving term and how the Kronecker delta delta_{i,c(j,ell)} selects it; also explain why the |1> (unflagged) component of O_A does not contribute.
reference_answer: Forward propagation of the source |0>|0^s>|j>: Apply D to the s-qubit register: |0>|0^s>|j> -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell |0>|ell>|j>. Apply O_A: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|A_{c(j,ell),j}|^2)|1>)|ell>|j>. Apply O_c (permuting the index register): -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|...|^2)|1>)|ell>|c(j,ell)>. Backward propagation of the target: instead of multiplying the leftmost (I tensor D tensor I) onto this line, apply it to |0>|0^s>|i>; since D is Hermitian, (I tensor D tensor I) on the left acts as D on |0^s> on the right of the bra, giving the ket (1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell'} |0>|ell'>|i>. Inner product: <0|<0^s|<i| U_A |0>|0^s>|j> = ((1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell'} <0|<ell'|<i|) ((1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|...|^2)|1>)|ell>|c(j,ell)>). The ancilla overlap <0 | (A|0> + sqrt(...)|1>) = A_{c(j,ell),j}, because <0|0> = 1 and <0|1> = 0 -- this is exactly why the |1> component drops out: the success flag <0| annihilates it. The s-register overlap <ell'|ell> = delta_{ell',ell} collapses the double sum to a single sum over ell. The index overlap <i|c(j,ell)> = delta_{i,c(j,ell)} keeps only the matching(s) ell for which c(j,ell) = i, i.e. the row that column j is matched to in matching ell equals the queried row i. Thus <0|<0^s|<i| U_A |0>|0^s>|j> = (1/s) sum_ell A_{c(j,ell),j} delta_{i,c(j,ell)} = (1/s) A_ij: if A_ij != 0 there is a unique ell with c(j,ell) = i (that nonzero entry lives in exactly one matching), contributing A_{i,j}; if A_ij = 0 no ell satisfies both the delta and a nonzero entry, so the sum is 0. The overall (1/s) is the LCU subnormalization. Hence U_A in BE_{s,s+1}(A).

question: An alternative s-sparse input model uses two (2n)-qubit oracles O_r |ell>|i> = |r(i,ell)>|i> and O_c |ell>|j> = |c(j,ell)>|j>, where r(i,ell) and c(j,ell) give the ell-th nonzero entry in row i and column j respectively, together with the entry oracle O_A |0>|i>|j> = (A_ij|0> + sqrt(1-|A_ij|^2)|1>)|i>|j> (controlled by both indices). The circuit of Fig. 9.8 applies D, O_c, O_A, then a SWAP, then D and O_r. Prove that the resulting U_A satisfies <0|<0^n|<i| U_A |0>|0^n|j> = (1/s) A_ij, so U_A in BE_{s,n+1}(A). In particular, explain the roles of the two separate delta constraints delta_{i,c(j,ell)} and delta_{r(i,ell'),j}, and why -- when A_ij = 0 -- the computation still gives 0 even though the rotation in O_A may be arbitrary on zero entries.
reference_answer: Propagate the source |0>|0^n>|j>. Apply D, O_c, O_A: |0>|0^n>|j> -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|A_{c(j,ell),j}|^2)|1>)|c(j,ell)>|j>, where O_c has written the matched row index c(j,ell) into the first register and O_A loaded the entry amplitude (controlled by the row c(j,ell) and column j). Apply SWAP, which exchanges the (row-like) and (column-like) registers: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (A_{c(j,ell),j}|0> + sqrt(1-|...|^2)|1>)|j>|c(j,ell)>. Propagate the target |0>|0^n>|i>. Apply D and O_r: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell'} |0>|r(i,ell')>|i>. Inner product: <0|<0^n|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|j> = (1/s) sum_{ell,ell'} A_{c(j,ell),j} <r(i,ell')|j> <i|c(j,ell)> (the ancilla <0| picks out A and kills the sqrt(1-|.|^2)|1> term). The two deltas: <i|c(j,ell)> = delta_{i,c(j,ell)} forces the matched row of column j in matching ell to be exactly i; <r(i,ell')|j> = delta_{r(i,ell'),j} forces the matched column of row i in matching ell' to be exactly j. Evaluate: = (1/s) sum_{ell,ell'} A_{c(j,ell),j} delta_{i,c(j,ell)} delta_{r(i,ell'),j}. If A_ij != 0, there is a unique ell with c(j,ell) = i (the nonzero (i,j) lies in exactly one column-matching) and a unique ell' with r(i,ell') = j (likewise for the row structure), so exactly one term survives, giving (1/s) A_{i,j} = (1/s) A_ij. If A_ij = 0: there is NO matching ell with c(j,ell) = i that carries a nonzero entry, and/or no ell' with r(i,ell') = j; hence for every (ell,ell') at least one delta is zero OR the surviving A_{c(j,ell),j} with c(j,ell) = i equals A_ij = 0. Either way the sum is 0. Crucially, even though O_A's rotation on a zero entry may be arbitrary (the text allows this), that arbitrary amplitude never contributes to the final matrix element: the two independent deltas from O_c and O_r only let a term survive when BOTH the column structure routes column j to row i and the row structure routes row i to column j, which happens only on genuine nonzero positions; on zero positions the position is simply not in the sparsity pattern so no (ell,ell') pair selects it. The joint row/column consistency is what makes the arbitrary zero-entry rotations harmless. Thus <0|<0^n|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|j> = (1/s) A_ij and U_A in BE_{s,n+1}(A).

question: A Hermitian matrix A does NOT automatically have a Hermitian block encoding: even for a Hermitian diagonal A and even when the approximation error is exactly 0, a generic (alpha, m, 0)-block-encoding U_A need not satisfy U_A = U_A^dagger -- only the upper-left n-qubit block of U_A is guaranteed Hermitian. (i) Explain precisely what the block-encoding definition does and does not constrain about U_A, so that Hermiticity of the encoded block does not propagate to the whole unitary. (ii) Give a concrete small example illustrating that the amplitude-oracle block encoding of a Hermitian diagonal matrix (Example 9.17) is generally not a Hermitian matrix. (iii) State what additional structural requirement defines a Hermitian block encoding (Definition 9.23) and why it is a strictly stronger condition useful for qubitization.
reference_answer: (i) The block-encoding definition only constrains the top-left n-qubit block: U_A in BE_{alpha,m}(A, 0) means (<0^m| tensor I) U_A (|0^m> tensor I) = A/alpha, i.e. it pins down the single sub-block indexed by ancilla = 0^m on both input and output. The remaining blocks (ancilla going 0^m -> nonzero, nonzero -> 0^m, and nonzero -> nonzero) are completely free apart from the global constraint that U_A be unitary. Hermiticity of A forces the top-left block to be Hermitian, but says nothing about the off-diagonal blocks or the complementary block; unitarity does not force those to make U_A self-adjoint. So A = A^dagger does not imply U_A = U_A^dagger. (ii) Example: take the 1x1-ancilla amplitude oracle for a diagonal A with a single real entry a = A_11 in (0,1). On the relevant 2x2 ancilla block (fixed index), U_A acts as the single-qubit rotation R = [[a, -sqrt(1-a^2)],[sqrt(1-a^2), a]] (a real rotation by angle theta with cos theta = a). This R is NOT symmetric/Hermitian: its off-diagonal entries are -sqrt(1-a^2) and +sqrt(1-a^2), which differ in sign, so R != R^T = R^dagger (for real R). The top-left entry is a = A_11 (Hermitian, trivially), yet the full U_A (a rotation, not a reflection) is not Hermitian. Thus even the block encoding of a Hermitian (indeed diagonal) matrix is generically non-Hermitian. (iii) Definition 9.23 adds the explicit requirement U_A = U_A^dagger: an (alpha,m,eps)-block-encoding that is ALSO a Hermitian matrix is called an (alpha,m,eps)-Hermitian-block-encoding (set HBE_{alpha,m}(A,eps)). This is strictly stronger: it is an extra global constraint on all blocks of U_A, not just the encoded sub-block, and generic block encodings (like the rotation above) violate it. It is useful for qubitization because when U_A = U_A^dagger each eigenvector |v_i> of A is 'qubitized' into a 2D invariant subspace H_i on which U_A acts as a reflection [[lambda_i, sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), -lambda_i]]; the self-adjointness is exactly what lets you apply U_A a second time to Eq. (9.30) and close the 2D subspace (Eq. (9.34)), which is the mechanism that turns U_A Z_Pi into a rotation implementing Chebyshev polynomials T_k(A). Without Hermiticity the simple reflection structure (and hence the clean two-step closure) is not available.

question: For an s-sparse Hermitian matrix A with ||A||_max <= 1, the Hermitian block-encoding circuit of Fig. 9.9 uses one location oracle O_c |ell>|j> = |c(j,ell)>|j>, an (n+1)-qubit SWAP, and a square-root entry oracle O_A |i>|0>|j> = |i>(sqrt(A_ij)|0> + sqrt(1 - |A_ij|)|1>)|j> acting on a single-qubit register, where for complex/negative entries one writes A_ij = |A_ij| e^{i theta_ij} and sqrt(A_ij) = sqrt(|A_ij|) e^{i theta_ij / 2}. Prove that the circuit yields <0|<0^n|<0|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|0>|j> = (1/s) A_ij, so U_A in HBE_{s,n+2}(A). You must show explicitly where Hermiticity A_ij = A_ji^* is used to combine the two square-root factors sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j}) and sqrt(A_{c(i,ell'),i})^* into A_ij.
reference_answer: Propagate the source |0>|0^n>|0>|j> through D, O_c, O_A: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell |0>|c(j,ell)>(sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j})|0> + sqrt(1-|A_{c(j,ell),j}|)|1>)|j>. Apply the (n+1)-qubit SWAP, which exchanges the first register pair (a,i) with the second (b,j): -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_ell (sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j})|0> + sqrt(1-|...|)|1>)|j>|0>|c(j,ell)>. Propagate the target |0>|0^n>|0>|i> through D, O_c, O_A: -> (1/sqrt(s)) sum_{ell'} |0>|c(i,ell')>(sqrt(A_{c(i,ell'),i})|0> + sqrt(1-|A_{c(i,ell'),i}|)|1>)|i>. Form the inner product <0|<0^n|<0|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|0>|j>. The two single-qubit ancillas each contribute a <0|(sqrt(A)|0> + sqrt(1-|A|)|1>) overlap, keeping only the sqrt(A)|0> part (the |1> terms are annihilated by <0|): one factor sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j}) from the source and, from the target bra, the conjugate sqrt(A_{c(i,ell'),i})^* (a bra conjugates amplitudes). The register overlaps give delta_{i,c(j,ell)} (target row index i must match the routed source index c(j,ell)) and delta_{c(i,ell'),j} (routed target index must match j). So <0|<0^n|<0|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|0>|j> = (1/s) sum_{ell,ell'} sqrt(A_{c(j,ell),j}) sqrt(A_{c(i,ell'),i})^* delta_{i,c(j,ell)} delta_{c(i,ell'),j}. When A_ij != 0 there is a unique ell with c(j,ell) = i and a unique ell' with c(i,ell') = j, so the surviving term is (1/s) sqrt(A_{i,j}) sqrt(A_{j,i})^*. Now use Hermiticity: A_ji = A_ij^*, hence sqrt(A_{j,i})^* = sqrt(A_ij^*)^* = sqrt(A_ij) (since conjugating the entry and then its square root returns the original square root: (sqrt(|A_ij|) e^{-i theta_ij/2})^* = sqrt(|A_ij|) e^{i theta_ij/2} = sqrt(A_ij)). Therefore sqrt(A_ij) sqrt(A_ji)^* = sqrt(A_ij) sqrt(A_ij) = (sqrt(A_ij))^2 = A_ij. This gives (1/s) A_ij, and when A_ij = 0 the deltas select no nonzero term, giving 0. Hence <0|<0^n|<0|<i| U_A |0>|0^n>|0>|j> = (1/s) A_ij for all i,j, so U_A in HBE_{s,n+2}(A). The two-register symmetric structure (source and target each run D, O_c, O_A, bridged by SWAP) is what makes U_A Hermitian, and Hermiticity of A is precisely what lets the two half-entries sqrt(A_{ij}) and sqrt(A_{ji})^* multiply back to the full entry A_ij.

question: The block-encoding notion generalizes beyond computational-basis subspaces. Fix rank-N and rank-N' orthogonal projectors Pi, Pi' on an ambient space C^{MN} (M = 2^m), with orthonormal bases {|phi_j>}_{j in [N]} for range(Pi) and {|psi_i>}_{i in [N']} for range(Pi'). Collect these as the first columns of unitaries Xi, Xi' and let Xi_N, (Xi')_{N'} be those column blocks. For a unitary U_A on C^{MN}, define the induced block A~ := ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger U_A Xi_N in C^{N' x N}. Prove that the (i,j) entry of A~ equals <psi_i| U_A |phi_j>, that A~ coincides with the compression Pi' U_A Pi expressed in the chosen bases, and hence that the exact relation Pi' U_A Pi = sum_{i,j} |psi_i> A_ij <phi_j| is equivalent to A~ = A. Then state the (alpha,m,eps)-generalized block-encoding condition ||A - alpha A~|| <= eps and explain why it reduces to the ordinary computational-basis definition when Pi = Pi' = |0^m><0^m| tensor I and N' = N.
reference_answer: Entry formula: Xi_N has columns |phi_0>,...,|phi_{N-1}>, so Xi_N |e_j> = |phi_j> for the standard basis vector |e_j> of C^N; similarly (Xi')_{N'} |e_i> = |psi_i>, hence ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger |x> has i-th component <psi_i|x>. Therefore the (i,j) entry of A~ = ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger U_A Xi_N is A~_{ij} = <e_i| ((Xi')_{N'})^dagger U_A Xi_N |e_j> = (((Xi')_{N'})|e_i>)^dagger U_A (Xi_N |e_j>) = <psi_i| U_A |phi_j>. Compression identity: the orthogonal projectors can be written Pi = sum_j |phi_j><phi_j| and Pi' = sum_i |psi_i><psi_i| (spectral form on their ranges). Then Pi' U_A Pi = sum_{i,j} |psi_i> <psi_i| U_A |phi_j> <phi_j| = sum_{i,j} |psi_i> A~_{ij} <phi_j|. So Pi' U_A Pi, re-expressed in the bases {|psi_i>}, {|phi_j>}, has exactly the matrix of coefficients A~. Consequently the exact encoding requirement Pi' U_A Pi = sum_{i,j} |psi_i> A_ij <phi_j| holds if and only if A~_{ij} = A_ij for all i,j, i.e. A~ = A. Approximate condition: allowing a subnormalization alpha and error eps, U_A is an (alpha,m,eps)-generalized block-encoding of A with respect to (Pi,Pi') iff ||A - alpha A~|| <= eps (operator norm), i.e. the compression alpha A~ = alpha Pi' U_A Pi (in the chosen bases) approximates A. Reduction to the usual definition: set Pi = Pi' = Pi_{0^m} := |0^m><0^m| tensor I and N' = N. Then range(Pi) = range(Pi') is the computational ancilla-0^m subspace; choosing Xi = Xi' = I (identity, whose first N columns are |0^m>|j>) gives Xi_N |e_j> = |0^m>|j> and (Xi')_{N'} |e_i> = |0^m>|i>, so A~_{ij} = <0^m|<i| U_A |0^m>|j>, which is exactly the standard top-left block (<0^m| tensor I) U_A (|0^m> tensor I). Thus ||A - alpha A~|| <= eps becomes the ordinary (alpha,m,eps)-block-encoding condition. The generalization is purely a change of input/output subspaces (via Pi, Pi' and the basis unitaries) from the fixed computational ancilla-flag subspace to arbitrary ones.

question: For a square matrix A with SVD A = W Sigma V^dagger, three generalized matrix functions are defined: f^diamond(A) = W f(Sigma) V^dagger (balanced), f^triangleright(A) = V f(Sigma) V^dagger (right), f^triangleleft(A) = W f(Sigma) W^dagger (left). The singular value transformation uses the diamond version for odd f and the right/triangleright version for even f. Prove that when A is Hermitian with eigendecomposition A = V D V^dagger (D indefinite, real), writing the SVD as A = W Sigma V^dagger with W = V sign(D) and Sigma = |D|, the singular value transformation f_SV(A) equals the ordinary eigenvalue transformation f(A) = V f(D) V^dagger whenever f has definite parity (odd or even). Treat the odd and even cases separately, and explain why definite parity is exactly the hypothesis that removes the sign ambiguity between singular values |lambda| and eigenvalues lambda.
reference_answer: Setup: A Hermitian gives A = V D V^dagger with real diagonal D = diag(lambda_i). Its SVD is A = W Sigma V^dagger with Sigma = |D| = diag(|lambda_i|) (singular values are nonnegative) and W = V sign(D), where sign(D) = diag(sign(lambda_i)) flips the sign of the i-th column of V whenever lambda_i < 0. One checks W Sigma V^dagger = V sign(D) |D| V^dagger = V D V^dagger = A, since sign(D)|D| = D. Odd case: f_SV(A) = f^diamond(A) = W f(Sigma) V^dagger = V sign(D) f(|D|) V^dagger. Now f(|D|) = diag(f(|lambda_i|)). Because f is odd, f(|lambda_i|) = sign(lambda_i) f(lambda_i) for each i: if lambda_i >= 0 then |lambda_i| = lambda_i and sign = +1; if lambda_i < 0 then f(|lambda_i|) = f(-lambda_i) = -f(lambda_i) = sign(lambda_i) f(lambda_i). Hence sign(D) f(|D|) = diag(sign(lambda_i) * sign(lambda_i) f(lambda_i)) = diag(f(lambda_i)) = f(D) (using sign(lambda_i)^2 = 1 for lambda_i != 0). Therefore f_SV(A) = V f(D) V^dagger = f(A). Even case: f_SV(A) = f^triangleright(A) = V f(Sigma) V^dagger = V f(|D|) V^dagger. Because f is even, f(|lambda_i|) = f(lambda_i) for every i (f(-x) = f(x)), so f(|D|) = f(D). Therefore f_SV(A) = V f(D) V^dagger = f(A). Role of definite parity: the SVD only sees |lambda_i| (the singular values are the absolute eigenvalues), discarding the sign carried by eigenvalues. To reconstruct f(A) = V f(D) V^dagger one must recover f(lambda_i) from f(|lambda_i|). This is possible exactly when the sign of f(lambda_i) relative to f(|lambda_i|) is determined by the sign of lambda_i in a fixed way: for odd f the sign flips with lambda_i (and the diamond's W = V sign(D) supplies precisely that flip), while for even f there is no sign to recover (f ignores it). For an f WITHOUT definite parity, f(lambda) and f(-lambda) are independent, so f(|lambda_i|) does not determine f(lambda_i) and the SVT cannot equal the eigenvalue transformation; definite parity is thus the exact structural hypothesis that eliminates the |lambda| vs lambda sign ambiguity.

question: For a general square matrix A with SVD given by A|v_i> = sigma_i|w_i>, A^dagger|w_i> = sigma_i|v_i>, sigma_i >= 0, define the one-ancilla dilated Hermitian matrix A~ = [[0, A^dagger],[A, 0]]. Define |z_i^pm> = (1/sqrt(2))(|0>|v_i> pm |1>|w_i>). Prove that A~ is Hermitian, that A~ |z_i^pm> = pm sigma_i |z_i^pm> (so the |z_i^pm> are a complete set of eigenvectors with eigenvalues pm sigma_i), and deduce that for an even function f, f(A~)|0>|psi> = |0> f^triangleright(A)|psi> while for an odd function f, f(A~)|0>|psi> = |1> f^diamond(A)|psi>. Explain how this shows that applying an eigenvalue transformation to the dilated matrix automatically realizes the singular value transformation of A, and why measuring the ancilla gives a definite outcome (0 for even f, 1 for odd f).
reference_answer: Hermiticity: A~^dagger = [[0, A^dagger],[A, 0]]^dagger = [[0, A^dagger],[A, 0]] = A~, since the (2,1) block A becomes (A^dagger)^dagger = A in position (1,2)... more precisely the adjoint swaps off-diagonal blocks and conjugate-transposes them: the (1,2) block A^dagger has adjoint A placed in (2,1), and the (2,1) block A has adjoint A^dagger placed in (1,2); these reproduce A~. So A~ is Hermitian. Eigenvectors: compute A~|z_i^pm> = (1/sqrt(2)) A~(|0>|v_i> pm |1>|w_i>). Using the block action A~(|0>|x>) = |1>(A|x>) and A~(|1>|y>) = |0>(A^dagger|y>) (the off-diagonal blocks move the ancilla and apply A or A^dagger): A~|0>|v_i> = |1>(A|v_i>) = sigma_i |1>|w_i>, and A~|1>|w_i> = |0>(A^dagger|w_i>) = sigma_i |0>|v_i>. Hence A~|z_i^pm> = (1/sqrt(2))(sigma_i|1>|w_i> pm sigma_i|0>|v_i>) = (sigma_i/sqrt(2))(pm|0>|v_i> + |1>|w_i>) = pm sigma_i * (1/sqrt(2))(|0>|v_i> pm |1>|w_i>) = pm sigma_i |z_i^pm>. So the |z_i^pm> are eigenvectors with eigenvalues pm sigma_i; as {|v_i>}, {|w_i>} are orthonormal bases, the {|z_i^pm>} form a complete orthonormal eigenbasis of the 2N-dimensional space. Matrix function: f(A~) = sum_i (|z_i^+> f(sigma_i) <z_i^+| + |z_i^-> f(-sigma_i) <z_i^-|). Expanding into the |0>,|1> blocks and using f_even(x) = (f(x)+f(-x))/2, f_odd(x) = (f(x)-f(-x))/2 gives f(A~) = [[ sum_i |v_i> f_even(sigma_i) <v_i|, sum_i |v_i> f_odd(sigma_i) <w_i| ],[ sum_i |w_i> f_odd(sigma_i) <v_i|, sum_i |w_i> f_even(sigma_i) <w_i| ]] = [[ f^triangleright_even(A), f^diamond_odd(A^dagger) ],[ f^diamond_odd(A), f^triangleleft_even(A) ]]. Now act on |0>|psi>: the |0> (ancilla) input picks out the first block-column. If f is EVEN, f_odd = 0, so f(A~)|0>|psi> = |0>(sum_i |v_i> f(sigma_i) <v_i|)|psi> = |0> f^triangleright(A)|psi>; the ancilla stays |0>. If f is ODD, f_even = 0, so f(A~)|0>|psi> = |1>(sum_i |w_i> f(sigma_i) <v_i|)|psi> = |1> f^diamond(A)|psi>; the ancilla flips to |1>. Interpretation: performing an eigenvalue transformation f on the Hermitian dilation A~ (which is what qubitization/QSVT does for Hermitian matrices) automatically produces, in the system register, the singular value transformation of A -- the diamond (odd) or triangleright (even) version -- because the eigenvalues of A~ are exactly the signed singular values pm sigma_i. The ancilla outcome is DEFINITE (0 for even, 1 for odd) because a definite-parity f kills one of the two parity components (f_odd or f_even), leaving the output entirely in a single ancilla branch; one therefore reads the ancilla deterministically and keeps the transformed system state with no postselection loss.

question: Not every eigenvalue transformation can be realized as a singular value transformation. Consider the matrix power f(x) = x^2 applied to a general diagonalizable but non-Hermitian matrix A = V D V^{-1} with SVD A = W Sigma V^dagger. Show by a concrete structural argument that A^2 generally CANNOT be written as a singular value transformation of A (i.e. as W g(Sigma) V^dagger, V g(Sigma) V^dagger, or W g(Sigma) W^dagger for any scalar g), by exhibiting the obstruction A^2 = W Sigma (V^dagger W) Sigma V^dagger in which the unitary factor V^dagger W does not simplify. Contrast this with the matrix inverse f(x) = x^{-1}, which IS a singular value transformation (A^{-1} = V Sigma^{-1} W^dagger = f_SV(A^dagger) with the odd f(x) = x^{-1}), and explain what property of the inverse makes it exceptional.
reference_answer: Write the SVD A = W Sigma V^dagger. Then A^2 = (W Sigma V^dagger)(W Sigma V^dagger) = W Sigma (V^dagger W) Sigma V^dagger. A singular value transformation produces one of W g(Sigma) V^dagger (balanced/diamond), V g(Sigma) V^dagger (right), or W g(Sigma) W^dagger (left): in each case the two outer unitary factors are W,V (or V,V or W,W) and the MIDDLE is a single diagonal function g(Sigma) of the singular values, with NO interior unitary between two Sigma factors. In A^2 = W Sigma (V^dagger W) Sigma V^dagger there is an interior unitary M := V^dagger W sandwiched between the two Sigma's. For a general non-Hermitian A, V and W are different unitaries and M = V^dagger W is a generic unitary that does not commute with Sigma and is not diagonal; hence Sigma M Sigma is not a function of Sigma alone -- it mixes the singular directions. There is no scalar g with Sigma M Sigma = g(Sigma) unless M is diagonal in the singular basis (which happens only in special cases, e.g. A normal so that V = W up to phases). Therefore A^2 cannot in general be put in any of the three SVT forms: the obstruction is precisely the non-trivial interior factor V^dagger W. (Concretely, for A = W Sigma V^dagger with Sigma = diag(2,1) and V^dagger W a 45-degree rotation, Sigma(V^dagger W)Sigma has off-diagonal entries, so it is not any diagonal g(Sigma).) Contrast -- the inverse is exceptional: A^{-1} = (W Sigma V^dagger)^{-1} = (V^dagger)^{-1} Sigma^{-1} W^{-1} = V Sigma^{-1} W^dagger (using V,W unitary). This has the diamond/SVT form with the outer unitaries V and W^dagger and middle diagonal Sigma^{-1} = g(Sigma) for g(x) = x^{-1}, and NO interior unitary. Equivalently, since f(x) = x^{-1} is ODD, f_SV(A^dagger) = f^diamond(A^dagger) = V Sigma^{-1} W^dagger = A^{-1}. What makes the inverse exceptional is that x^{-1} is a function applied to EACH singular value independently and the inversion of a product of unitaries-times-diagonal reverses the order WITHOUT inserting any interior unitary between two diagonals -- there is only ONE Sigma factor to transform, so no V^dagger W cross term ever appears. Powers A^k for k >= 2 (and matrix exp, log, etc.) involve PRODUCTS of A, each contributing its own W,Sigma,V^dagger, which forces interior V^dagger W factors; the inverse (a single reciprocal) is the one monomial that avoids this.

The exp/log non-SVT remarks match the source's own claim by analogy. Structural obstruction argument correct. Correct counterexample. Distinct core.

question: Let U_A in HBE_{1,m}(A) be a Hermitian block encoding of a Hermitian A with ||A|| <= 1, spectral decomposition A = sum_i lambda_i |v_i><v_i|, so that U_A |0^m>|v_i> = lambda_i |0^m>|v_i> + sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)|perp_i> with Pi|perp_i> = 0, Pi = |0^m><0^m| tensor I. For -1 < lambda_i < 1, prove that H_i = span{|0^m>|v_i>, |perp_i>} is a 2D invariant subspace of U_A on which U_A is a reflection [[lambda_i, sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), -lambda_i]], that the iterate O = U_A Z_Pi (with Z_Pi = 2 Pi - I) acts on H_i as the rotation [[lambda_i, -sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), lambda_i]], and hence that O^k restricted to H_i has top-left entry T_k(lambda_i) (Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind), so O^k = (U_A Z_Pi)^k is a (1,m,0)-block-encoding of T_k(A). State where Hermiticity of U_A is used.
reference_answer: Invariant subspace and reflection form: by the HBE relation, U_A|0^m>|v_i> = lambda_i|0^m>|v_i> + sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)|perp_i>, with |perp_i> normalized and orthogonal to the Pi-subspace. Since U_A is Hermitian (U_A = U_A^dagger) and U_A is unitary, U_A^2 = I. Apply U_A again to the identity above: U_A(U_A|0^m>|v_i>) = |0^m>|v_i>, i.e. lambda_i U_A|0^m>|v_i> + sqrt(1-lambda_i^2) U_A|perp_i> = |0^m>|v_i>. Substituting U_A|0^m>|v_i> and solving gives U_A|perp_i> = sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)|0^m>|v_i> - lambda_i|perp_i>. Thus both U_A|0^m>|v_i> and U_A|perp_i> lie in H_i = span{|0^m>|v_i>, |perp_i>}, so H_i is invariant, and in the ordered basis B_i = {|0^m>|v_i>, |perp_i>} the matrix of U_A is [[lambda_i, sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), -lambda_i]], a (symmetric, trace-0, determinant -1) reflection. Hermiticity is used precisely here: applying U_A = U_A^dagger a SECOND time (via U_A^2 = I) is what produces the closed expression for U_A|perp_i> and hence the 2D invariance; without Hermiticity U_A|perp_i> need not stay in H_i. Iterate as rotation: H_i is invariant for Pi too, with [Pi]_{B_i} = [[1,0],[0,0]] (since |0^m>|v_i> is in range(Pi) and |perp_i> is orthogonal to it). Hence Z_Pi = 2Pi - I has [Z_Pi]_{B_i} = [[1,0],[0,-1]], a reflection. The iterate O = U_A Z_Pi has matrix [[lambda_i, sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), -lambda_i]] [[1,0],[0,-1]] = [[lambda_i, -sqrt(1-lambda_i^2)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2), lambda_i]], which with lambda_i = cos theta_i is exactly the rotation [[cos theta_i, -sin theta_i],[sin theta_i, cos theta_i]] (product of two reflections = rotation). Chebyshev powers: therefore [O^k]_{B_i} = [[cos k theta_i, -sin k theta_i],[sin k theta_i, cos k theta_i]] = [[T_k(lambda_i), -sqrt(1-lambda_i^2) U_{k-1}(lambda_i)],[sqrt(1-lambda_i^2) U_{k-1}(lambda_i), T_k(lambda_i)]], using T_k(cos theta) = cos(k theta) and U_{k-1}(cos theta) = sin(k theta)/sin theta. The top-left entry is T_k(lambda_i). Block encoding of T_k(A): the vectors {|0^m>|v_i>} span range(Pi), and on each H_i the (0^m,0^m) component of O^k equals T_k(lambda_i). Summing over i, Pi O^k Pi = sum_i T_k(lambda_i) |0^m>|v_i><v_i|<0^m| = |0^m><0^m| tensor T_k(A). Hence (<0^m| tensor I) O^k (|0^m> tensor I) = T_k(A), i.e. O^k = (U_A Z_Pi)^k in BE_{1,m,0}(T_k(A)). native_nl.core_summary: In an eight-counter exact-real operation model, prove a stored two-row plane rotation on length-M rows costs exactly 6*M field, 10*M read and 6*M write operations, accounting for each from the three materialized passes.

question: Work in an exact-real word-operation model that keeps eight separate running counters: field operations, square roots, inverse-cosine calls, other trigonometric calls, exact comparisons, stored-word reads, stored-word writes, and emitted records. Each primitive call adds one unit to its own counter; proof checking, counter bookkeeping and loop-index arithmetic are free, and stored data are nested vectors. A plane rotation acts on two stored length-M real rows u and v with coefficients c and s, returning rows whose j-th entries are c*u_j - s*v_j and s*u_j + c*v_j. The implementation first materializes a stored vector of M computed entry-pairs, then materializes the first output row and the second output row as two further stored passes. Every materialized pass over M indices additionally charges two reads and two writes per index to write each intermediate value and read it back for projection, and each single entry-pair is computed with exactly the six field operations c*u_j, s*v_j, s*u_j, c*v_j, their difference, and their sum. Prove that rotating the two rows costs exactly 6*M field operations, 10*M reads and 6*M writes, and account for the origin of every read and write.
reference_answer: Count the three materialized passes separately. Pass 1 computes the entry-pairs: for each index j it reads u_j and v_j (2 reads) and performs the six field operations, so its own work is 6 field + 2 reads per index; the materialization surcharge adds 2 reads + 2 writes per index, giving 6*M field + 4*M reads + 2*M writes. Pass 2 materializes the first output row by reading the stored pair at each index (1 read) and projecting its first component (free), with surcharge 2 reads + 2 writes, giving 3*M reads + 2*M writes. Pass 3 does the same for the second component, another 3*M reads + 2*M writes. Summing: field = 6*M; reads = 4*M + 3*M + 3*M = 10*M; writes = 2*M + 2*M + 2*M = 6*M. The field count is purely the arithmetic of the rotation; the reads split into 2*M genuine input reads, 2*M pair reads for the two projections, and 6*M materialization read-backs; the writes are the three stored passes at 2*M each. This is an exact operation count in the extended exact-real model, not a finite-bit running-time bound, and it does not assert that any of these operations is physically free.

question: In the eight-counter exact-real model, a column sweep eliminates entries below a pivot by performing a chronological chain of elimination steps. Each step first computes an elimination angle and the two rotation coefficients (bounded by a fixed per-step budget B that is independent of which branch of the angle computation is taken), applies a rotation to the stored matrix, and then emits exactly one rotation record (one unit on the emitted-record counter). A sweep performing k steps is defined by recursion: zero steps emit nothing and do no work; a sweep of k+1 steps performs one elimination step and then recurses on the resulting matrix, emitting one record for the step. Prove by induction on k that (a) the total cost of a k-step sweep is at most k*(B + one emit) on every counter, and (b) the emitted-record counter equals exactly k, even though some steps may rotate by a harmless zero angle.
reference_answer: Argue by induction on the number of steps k. Base case k=0: the sweep returns the input unchanged with zero cost on every counter, so both the bound 0*(B+emit) and the exact emit count 0 hold. Inductive step k+1: by the recursive definition the sweep cost equals the cost of one elimination step, plus the cost of the k-step sweep on the updated matrix, plus one emitted record. For (a), the single step is bounded by B on every counter (the per-step budget already absorbs the branch-independent angle budget, both rotation coefficients, the rotation, and the stored reads), the recursive part is bounded by k*(B+emit) by the induction hypothesis, and the emit contributes one unit; adding gives at most (k+1)*(B+emit) on every counter. For (b), the single step emits exactly one record and the recursive sweep emits exactly k by hypothesis, with no other operation touching the emit counter, so the total is exactly k+1. The exact emit equality holds regardless of the actual angles because a zero-angle rotation still produces and emits its record; the step budget B is only an upper bound on the arithmetic counters, so the two claims are of different strengths: an exact count for emissions and an inequality for the rest.

question: In the eight-counter exact-real model, a bounded sum over an index set of size k is evaluated by a monadic fold: starting from the pure value zero (no charge), each of the k summands is produced and then added to the running accumulator with one field addition. Suppose every summand has the same per-counter cost B. Prove that the whole sum costs exactly k*(B + one field operation). Then specialize to a single contraction entry over a bond of size D, where each summand reads one entry of a stored core (two reads) and one entry of a stored vector (one read) and multiplies them (one field), so B is three reads plus one field, and conclude that the entry costs exactly D*(three reads + two field operations).

Inductive step: a sum over k+1 indices produces the first summand (cost B), binds an addition of it to the recursively evaluated tail (that addition is one field operation), and the tail is a sum over k indices. By the induction hypothesis the tail costs k*(B+field); adding the first summand's B and the one field for its combination gives B + field + k*(B+field) = (k+1)*(B+field). So the sum costs exactly k*(B+field) on every counter. For the contraction entry: each summand reads a stored core entry, which is a row read followed by an entry read (two reads), reads one stored vector entry (one read), and multiplies the two values (one field), so B = three reads + one field. Substituting into the law gives D*((three reads + one field) + one field) = D*(three reads + two field operations). The second field per index is exactly the accumulation addition, which is why the entry has two field operations per bond index rather than one. This is an exact count in the extended exact-real model, not a finite-bit cost.

question: Two notions of total cost appear in the stored exact-real model. One, call it the ordinary total, is the sum of a cost function over the finite type of all operation tags. The other, call it the enumerated total, is the explicit eight-term sum field + square root + inverse-cosine + other-trig + comparison + read + write + emitted-record. Prove that these two totals are equal as functions of the cost, that the total of a sum of two costs is the sum of their totals, that the total of the zero cost is zero, and that the total of a single unit charge on one tag is one. reference_answer: The operation tags form a finite type with exactly the eight inhabitants field, square root, inverse-cosine, other-trig, comparison, read, write, emitted-record. The ordinary total sums the cost over the universal finite set of tags. Enumerating that finite set as the eight listed inhabitants, the sum over the set equals field + sqrt + angle + trig + compare + read + write + emit, which is precisely the enumerated total; hence the two totals coincide for every cost. Additivity: the sum over tags of (a+b) applied pointwise is the sum over tags of a plus the sum over tags of b, because finite summation distributes over pointwise addition; so the total of a sum is the sum of the totals. Zero: the zero cost assigns zero to every tag, and a finite sum of zeros is zero. Unit charge: a single unit charge on one tag assigns one to that tag and zero to the others, so its total over all tags is exactly one. These facts matter because cost expressions are built compositionally by adding sub-costs and charging unit ticks; additivity lets a total be computed term by term, the zero and unit laws evaluate the leaves, and the enumeration identity lets a proof pass freely between the abstract sum-over-tags and the concrete eight-term polynomial used in the final bound. All of this concerns operation counts in the exact-real model and makes no finite-bit runtime claim.

question: A primitive quantum circuit is a chronological list of gates, each gate acting on a set of touched wires. A per-wire scheduling fold tracks, for every wire, the earliest layer at which its next gate can be placed: processing a gate pushes every touched wire to one more than the maximum current depth over the gate's touched wires, and leaves untouched wires unchanged. The circuit depth is the maximum over all wires of the final per-wire depths; the gate count is the length of the list. Prove that the circuit depth is at most the gate count, i.e. that scheduling in parallel layers never makes the reported depth exceed the number of gates. reference_answer: The key per-step fact is: if every wire currently has depth at most some bound, then after processing one gate every wire has depth at most that bound plus one. For a touched wire the new depth is one plus the maximum current depth over the touched wires; since each of those is at most the bound, their maximum is at most the bound, so the new depth is at most bound plus one. For an untouched wire the depth is unchanged, hence at most the bound and so at most bound plus one. Now induct on the gate list to bound the folded profile: starting from the all-zero profile (every wire at most 0), each of the L gates raises the uniform upper bound by at most one, so after the whole circuit every wire has depth at most 0 + L = L, the gate count. Taking the maximum over wires, the circuit depth is at most L. Finally the reported resource depth is defined to equal this scheduling depth, so it too is at most the gate count. This bounds a genuine parallel-scheduling depth, computed by the per-wire fold rather than assigned as a serial surrogate; equality can fail because parallelizable gates on disjoint wires share a layer, making the true depth strictly smaller than the gate count.

question: A stored N-by-M matrix is built by materializing an entry supplier: for each of the N*M entries the supplier is run to produce a value, and the construction charges, on top of the supplier's own counted work, two reads and two writes per entry plus two reads and two writes per row to store and project. reference_answer: The claim is false because the cost identity contains the double sum of the supplier's own per-entry costs, which is not determined by N and M alone. Counterexample: let the supplier for entry (i,j) perform j additional field operations (say by summing j stored values before returning). Then the supplier's per-entry cost is not constant, and the double sum of field operations equals the sum over i of (0+1+...+(M-1)) = N*M*(M-1)/2 field operations, which depends on the internal structure of the supplier, not merely on the surcharge. Two different suppliers producing matrices of the same dimensions can therefore have different total costs, so no fixed polynomial in N and M alone bounds every materialization. Indeed the source flags the input callback as an explicit boundary: the constructor charges storage but does not certify the callback's scalar evaluation cost. The correct statement is conditional: if the supplier's per-entry cost is bounded by a uniform value B on every counter, then the materialization is bounded by N*M*B plus (N*M + N) times the surcharge; only after supplying such a per-entry bound B does a polynomial-in-dimensions bound follow. All of this is in the exact-real operation model and makes no finite-bit claim; the moral is that materialization cost cleanly separates the surcharge (fixed by dimensions) from the supplier work (which must be separately bounded).

Then the squared norm is 0, its square root is 0, the zero test succeeds, and the routine returns the angle zero immediately, performing zero inverse-cosine calls, zero divisions, and no sign test. So on this input the actual inverse-cosine count is 0, not 1, contradicting the claim that every call makes exactly one inverse-cosine call. The source states the budget bound as an inequality, holding on every counter for all inputs; it is explicitly described as a branch-independent upper bound in which the zero pair uses fewer operations. The correct relationship is: the budget is an over-approximation that is tight only on the nonzero branch, where the division, inverse-cosine, sign test and the arithmetic for signing and doubling are all executed. On the zero branch several counters are strictly below their budget. Hence one may use the budget to bound sums of many angle computations, but may not read it as an exact per-call cost; exactness holds only for the emit-style counters elsewhere, not for the arithmetic counters of the angle routine. This is an exact-real operation-count distinction, with no finite-bit runtime content.

Step 1: the Taylor coefficients of P about a are read off directly: the coefficient of (x-a)^j is v(j)/j! for j <= k and 0 for j > k, because P is already written in the (x-a) basis. Step 2: apply the bridge at order j <= k: (d^j P/dx^j)(a) = j! * (coefficient of (x-a)^j) = j! * (v(j)/j!). Step 3: since j! is a nonzero natural number cast into the reals, j! * (v(j)/j!) = v(j) exactly. Hence every requested jet value is reproduced, and the construction has degree at most k, has degree at most k. The bound k is the generic (worst-case) degree needed to carry k+1 derivative constraints at a single node; particular data may be realised by a lower-degree polynomial (all-zero data gives the zero polynomial, and if v(k)=0 the degree drops below k), so k is an upper bound on this construction's degree, not a universal minimum for every data vector. question: Let p and q be real polynomials and a a real point. Suppose (x-a)^{k+1} divides the difference p-q. Step 1 (differentiation lowers the zero order by at most j): differentiating a function with a zero of order m at a exactly j times leaves a zero of order at least m-j; formally, (x-a)^{m-j} divides the j-th derivative of r whenever (x-a)^m | r. With m = k+1 and j <= k we get m-j = k+1-j >= 1. Step 2: therefore (x-a)^{k+1-j} divides (d^j r/dx^j); since k+1-j >= 1, in particular (x-a)^1 = (x-a) divides the j-th derivative of r. Step 3: a polynomial divisible by (x-a) vanishes at a; evaluating (d^j r/dx^j) at a gives 0. Step 4: derivatives are linear, so (d^j r/dx^j)(a) = (d^j p/dx^j)(a) - (d^j q/dx^j)(a) = 0, i.e. the jets agree. Why only below the multiplicity: at j = k+1 we have m-j = 0, so the argument only yields (x-a)^0 = 1 dividing the derivative, a vacuous statement; the (k+1)-th derivatives need not agree.
