question: Prove the classical query lower bound for unstructured search: for a Boolean function on n-bit strings promised to have a unique marked input, no unbiased classical algorithm can identify the marked input with probability greater than one half using fewer than two-to-the-n minus one queries in the worst case. Make explicit the role of the padding-to-a-fixed-number-of-queries reduction and the indistinguishability-of-two-candidates argument. Then state why this does NOT by itself establish any quantum lower bound.
reference_answer: Let the domain have two-to-the-n = N strings and suppose, for contradiction, an unbiased algorithm identifies the unique marked string using at most N minus two queries in the worst case. First, pad: if the algorithm sometimes uses fewer than N minus two queries, append arbitrary extra queries up to exactly N minus two; this cannot hurt, because once the marked string is found all later queries return zero on non-marked inputs and reveal nothing new, so without loss of generality the algorithm always makes exactly N minus two queries with distinct inputs x_1, through x_{N-2}. Those N minus two queried inputs leave exactly two unqueried strings; call them x-star and x-prime. Consider the two worlds in which the marked string is x-star versus x-prime. In BOTH worlds every queried input is unmarked, so every query returns zero: the observed evidence f(x_1) = ... = f(x_{N-2}) = 0 is identical in the two worlds. Therefore the algorithm's output distribution is the same whether the answer is x-star or x-prime, so it cannot distinguish them; any fixed guess is correct in at most one of the two equally consistent worlds, giving success probability at most one half on this pair. Hence to exceed one half the algorithm must make at least N minus one queries, which is the claimed bound. The padding reduction is what lets us assume a fixed query count so that exactly two candidates remain; the indistinguishability argument is what forces the one-half ceiling, because identical evidence cannot support a better-than-even decision between two equally likely hypotheses. Why this gives no quantum lower bound: the argument counts classical queries each returning one deterministic bit and relies on the evidence being a fixed set of zero/one answers. A quantum algorithm queries the oracle in superposition, so a single quantum query can probe all inputs coherently and the evidence is not a list of classical bit answers; the counting of distinguishable classical transcripts does not apply. Establishing a quantum lower bound requires a genuinely quantum argument (such as a hybrid/adversary method), and indeed the quantum query complexity is only order the square root of N, far below the classical N minus one.

question: The marking information for search is first given as a bit oracle that adds the function value into an answer qubit modulo two. Prove that running this bit oracle with the answer qubit prepared in the minus state converts it into a phase oracle that multiplies each input basis state by minus one exactly when it is marked, leaving the answer qubit unchanged. Make explicit why this is a clean conversion (the answer qubit factorizes out and can be reused), and explain the resource consequence: that one phase-oracle reflection costs one bit-oracle query plus state preparation of the answer qubit, with no measurement or amplification required.
reference_answer: Prepare the answer qubit in the minus state, the equal superposition of zero and one with a relative minus sign, normalized by one over the square root of two. The bit oracle maps an input string x with answer bit y to the same x with answer bit y exclusive-or f(x). Apply it to x tensored with the minus state: by linearity it sends the minus state's two components, (x,0) with plus sign and (x,1) with minus sign, to (x, f(x)) with plus sign and (x, 1 exclusive-or f(x)) with minus sign. If f(x) = 0 this is (x,0) plus sign and (x,1) minus sign, i.e. x tensored with the minus state unchanged. If f(x) = 1 this is (x,1) with plus sign and (x,0) with minus sign, i.e. x tensored with (minus the minus state) = (minus one) times x tensored with the minus state. In both cases the result is (minus one) to the f(x) times x tensored with the minus state. Hence the overall action is x tensored with minus state mapping to (minus one) to the f(x) times the same, which is exactly a phase oracle applying the sign (minus one) to the f(x) on the input register while the answer qubit is returned unchanged in the minus state. The conversion is clean because the answer qubit comes out in the identical minus state regardless of x, so it factorizes completely out of the input register and is left unentangled; therefore it can be prepared once and reused across every application of the phase oracle (including both the marked-state reflection and, by the same device, the diffusion reflection). Resource consequence: one application of the phase-oracle reflection costs exactly one query to the bit oracle plus the one-time preparation of the answer qubit in the minus state (a single-qubit state preparation), and crucially it requires no measurement and no amplification, because phase kickback is a unitary, deterministic effect; the sign is imprinted coherently rather than read out. Thus converting bit access to phase access is free up to a reusable ancilla, and the search's query accounting can be stated directly in phase-oracle reflections.

question: Amplitude amplification generalizes Grover search to a good subspace defined by a projector, where a state-preparation unitary produces a state whose overlap with the good subspace has magnitude equal to the square root of the initial success probability. Suppose this initial success probability is a small positive number p (for example the fraction of good states). (a) Prove that the amplitude-based reflection scheme increases the good-subspace amplitude per iteration by an amount of order the square root of p, whereas naive classical repetition increases the accumulated success probability only linearly in p per trial. (b) Deduce that reaching a constant success probability needs order one over the square root of p amplitude-amplification iterations against order one over p classical trials, and explain precisely why working with amplitudes rather than probabilities is the origin of the quadratic speedup. Keep the comparison at the level of queries to the state-preparation unitary and the good-subspace reflection.
reference_answer: Set the half-angle so that the sine of the half-angle equals the square root of p; this is the overlap magnitude of the prepared state with the good subspace. (a) The amplitude-amplification iterate is, as in Grover, a product of two reflections (the reflection about the good subspace and the reflection about the prepared state), hence a rotation by the full angle equal to twice the half-angle in the two-dimensional plane spanned by the good and bad components. Each iteration therefore rotates the state vector by the fixed angle twice the half-angle; for small p the half-angle is approximately the square root of p, so each iteration increases the good-direction amplitude (the sine of the running angle) by an increment of order twice the square root of p near the start. In contrast, classical repetition does not rotate an amplitude: each independent trial succeeds with probability p and the probability of having succeeded at least once after t trials is one minus (one minus p) to the t, which for small p grows like p times t, i.e. the accumulated success PROBABILITY increases linearly in p per trial. So one quantum iteration buys an amplitude increment of order the square root of p, while one classical trial buys a probability increment of order p. (b) To reach a constant good-direction amplitude (success probability of order one) the running angle must reach order a right angle; since each iteration advances the angle by order the square root of p, the number of iterations needed is order a right angle divided by the square root of p, i.e. order one over the square root of p iterations, each costing one query to the state-preparation unitary (and its adjoint) and one good-subspace reflection. Classically, reaching constant cumulative success probability needs p times t of order one, i.e. t of order one over p trials, each costing one state preparation and one check. The ratio is one over the square root of p against one over p, a quadratic saving. The origin of the quadratic speedup is precisely that the quantum procedure manipulates the AMPLITUDE, which grows linearly in the number of iterations at rate the square root of p, while the measured probability is the SQUARE of the amplitude; so when the amplitude reaches order one the probability also reaches order one, but the amplitude only had to travel a distance set by the square root of p, not p. Equivalently, a rotation by an angle of order the square root of p per step reaches a right angle in order one over the square root of p steps, and Born's rule converts the linear-in-steps amplitude growth into the quadratic advantage over probability-based classical sampling. All costs are counted in state-preparation-unitary and good-subspace-reflection calls.

question: Let V and W be finite-dimensional complex vector spaces and identify End(V tensor W) with End(V) tensor End(W). Consider the subalgebra A consisting of operators of the form a tensor 1 with a in End(V), where 1 is the identity on W. Prove that the commutant of A inside End(V tensor W), that is the set of all operators commuting with every element of A, is exactly the set of operators 1 tensor b with b in End(W).
reference_answer: Write n for the dimension of W and fix a basis of W, so every operator T on V tensor W becomes an n-by-n block matrix with blocks that are endomorphisms of V. In this basis a tensor 1 is block diagonal with the single block a repeated on the diagonal. First inclusion: any operator 1 tensor b has blocks that are scalar multiples of the identity on V, namely the entry of b times the identity, and these commute with the block-diagonal a tensor 1 because scalars commute with a; so every 1 tensor b lies in the commutant. Second inclusion: suppose a block operator T commutes with a tensor 1 for all a in End(V). Comparing blocks, the (i,j) block of (a tensor 1) T is a times the (i,j) block of T, while that of T (a tensor 1) is the (i,j) block of T times a, so block times a equals a times block for every a in End(V) and every pair i,j. An operator on V that commutes with all of End(V) must be a scalar multiple of the identity (apply the relation to rank-one operators, or use that the defining action of End(V) on V is irreducible). Hence each block equals a scalar times the identity on V, which means T = 1 tensor c where c in End(W) collects those scalars. Therefore the commutant equals the operators 1 tensor b, as claimed.

question: Let a finite group act on a finite-dimensional space V with isotypical decomposition V = direct sum over alpha of (V_alpha tensor C^{n_alpha}) into pairwise inequivalent irreducible pieces V_alpha appearing with multiplicity n_alpha. Let A be the algebra of operators generated by the representation. Prove that the commutant A' equals the direct sum over alpha of (1 on V_alpha, tensored with End(C^{n_alpha})), and deduce that the double commutant equals A.
reference_answer: The isotypical projections onto the summands V_alpha tensor C^{n_alpha} lie in A, so any element b of the commutant A' commutes with each such projection and is therefore block diagonal: b is a direct sum of pieces b_alpha, each an endomorphism of V_alpha tensor C^{n_alpha}. On the alpha block the algebra A restricts to (End(V_alpha) tensored with the identity on the multiplicity space): the irreducible action on V_alpha with the multiplicity factor left untouched. By the commutant lemma for a tensor product, the commutant of (End(V_alpha) tensor identity) inside End(V_alpha tensor C^{n_alpha}) is (identity on V_alpha, tensored with End(C^{n_alpha})); hence each b_alpha has this form and A' is the stated direct sum. Conversely every such operator commutes with A, so this is an equality. Applying the same commutant lemma a second time: the commutant of (identity on V_alpha tensor End(C^{n_alpha})) inside each block is (End(V_alpha) tensor identity), and summing over alpha shows the double commutant equals the direct sum of (End(V_alpha) tensor identity), which is A. Thus the bicommutant recovers A.

question: Given representations (phi, V) of a group G and (psi, W) of a group H, the external product representation of the direct product G cross H acts on V tensor W by sending the pair (g,h) to phi(g) tensor psi(h). Explain precisely how this differs from the inner tensor representation of a single group acting on V tensor W, and give the reasoning behind the two standard facts: that the external product of two irreducible representations is irreducible, and that every irreducible representation of G cross H arises this way.
reference_answer: In the external product the two tensor factors are driven by independent group elements: the pair (g,h) acts as phi(g) tensor psi(h). In the inner tensor representation of a single group G on V tensor W the same element g acts as phi(g) tensor phi(g), so both factors move together; the two constructions use different groups and are not the same action. Irreducibility of an external product of irreducibles: the character of the external product factorizes as the product of the two characters, chi(g,h) = chi over V of g, times chi over W of h, and the averaged squared modulus of a character over G cross H factorizes as the product of the averaged squared moduli over G and over H separately. Each factor equals one when V and W are irreducible, so the averaged squared modulus of chi is one, which is exactly the irreducibility criterion. Exhaustion: the number of external products of irreducibles equals the number of irreducibles of G times that of H, which equals the number of conjugacy classes of G times that of H; a conjugacy class of the product group is a product of a class in each factor, so this count is the number of conjugacy classes of G cross H, hence the number of its irreducibles. Since the external products are distinct irreducibles and there are exactly that many, they exhaust all irreducibles of the product group.

question: On the n-fold tensor power of V = C^d let the symmetric group S_n act by permuting tensor factors, spanning an algebra A, and let the general linear group GL(V) act diagonally by sending U to the n-fold tensor power of U, spanning an algebra B. Assume it is already known that the commutant A' equals the span of all operators of the form the n-fold tensor power of a single endomorphism X of V. Prove that B equals A', and conclude using the double commutant theorem that the commutant of B equals A.
reference_answer: First B is contained in A': each diagonal operator (the n-fold power of a unitary) commutes with every factor permutation, so B commutes with A and lies in A'. For the reverse inclusion we show every generator of A', namely the n-fold power of an arbitrary endomorphism X, lies in B, including non-invertible X. Fix X in End(V). For all but finitely many scalars t the operator X + t times the identity is invertible, hence its n-fold tensor power lies in B for those t. Now view the map sending t to the n-fold tensor power of (X + t times identity) as a function of t: expanding the product it is a polynomial in t of degree n whose coefficients are fixed operators (the symmetrized partial tensor terms). A polynomial of degree n taking values in the subspace B at more than n distinct points must have every coefficient in B, so by Lagrange interpolation the entire curve lies in B for all t, in particular at t = 0, giving the n-fold power of X in B. Thus A', the span of these powers, is contained in B, and together with B contained in A' we get B = A'. Finally the double commutant theorem gives the bicommutant of A equal to A; since that bicommutant is the commutant of A' = B, we conclude the commutant of B equals A.

question: Let V be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let the symmetric subspace of its n-fold tensor power be the set of tensors fixed by every permutation of the n factors. Prove that this symmetric subspace equals the span of the n-fold powers of single vectors v of V.
reference_answer: Call the span of the single-vector powers W. One inclusion is immediate: each n-fold power of a single vector is unchanged by any factor permutation, so W is contained in the symmetric subspace. For the reverse inclusion, start from the standard spanning set of the symmetric subspace obtained by symmetrizing basis tensors: for a basis of V the symmetrized basis tensors, each a sum over all permutations of a fixed arrangement of basis vectors, span the symmetric subspace. These symmetrized tensors are polarizations: each equals a mixed partial derivative, evaluated at the origin, of the single-vector power of a vector of the form (first basis vector plus t_2 times second plus ... plus t_n times last), differentiated once in each of t_2, ..., t_n. Each such derivative is a limit of difference quotients of elements that are themselves n-fold powers of single vectors, all of which lie in W. Because V is finite-dimensional, W is a finite-dimensional and hence closed subspace, so these limits remain in W. Therefore every symmetrizer, and thus the whole symmetric subspace, lies in W, giving equality.

question: In the Schur-Weyl decomposition of the n-fold tensor power of C^d, only Young diagrams with at most d rows contribute. reference_answer: Fix a standard tableau T of shape lambda and a tensor basis vector v obtained by choosing one basis label from the alphabet of size d for each of the n factors. Record the labels into the diagram by writing the label from factor j into the box that carries the number j in T; call the result the filled tableau of v. The Young symmetrizer is the product of row symmetrization followed by column antisymmetrization, and the column antisymmetrization carries the sign of each column permutation. Suppose lambda has p rows with p greater than d. Then the first column has p boxes, but the labels placed in them are drawn from the d-element alphabet; since p is greater than d, by the pigeonhole principle two boxes in the first column receive the same label. Antisymmetrizing a column that contains two equal entries gives zero: the transposition swapping those two equal boxes fixes v yet contributes a factor of minus one, so the antisymmetrized sum cancels in pairs. Hence the symmetrizer sends v to zero for every basis vector v, so it annihilates the whole tensor power and the piece associated with lambda is absent. The decisive mechanism is the column antisymmetrization combined with pigeonhole on a d-letter alphabet; this is exactly why diagrams need at most d rows.

question: Let P be the antisymmetrizing projector on the n-fold tensor power of C^d, defined as the average over S_n of the sign of a permutation times the corresponding factor permutation. Prove that if d is strictly less than n then P annihilates the entire space, and interpret this as the statement that the totally antisymmetric subspace of the tensor power is zero whenever n exceeds d.
reference_answer: The image of P is the totally antisymmetric subspace, consisting of tensors that pick up the sign of any permutation when their factors are permuted. A spanning set for this image is obtained by antisymmetrizing basis tensors; the antisymmetrization of a basis tensor is, up to a scalar, the wedge of the chosen basis vectors. If two of the chosen indices coincide, this wedge is zero, because the transposition exchanging the two equal factors both fixes the tensor and multiplies it by minus one, forcing it to vanish. A nonzero antisymmetrized basis tensor therefore requires all n indices to be distinct, i.e. a strictly increasing choice of n labels drawn from the d-element alphabet. When n is greater than d there is no such choice: any n labels from a d-element set must repeat by the pigeonhole principle. Hence every antisymmetrized basis tensor is zero, the spanning set is trivial, the antisymmetric subspace is the zero subspace, and P is the zero operator. Equivalently its rank is the number of n-element subsets of a d-element set, which is zero for n greater than d.

question: Fix a standard Young tableau T of shape lambda, a partition of n into at most d parts, and a tensor basis vector v of the n-fold tensor power of C^d. reference_answer: Claim: the Young symmetrizer annihilates v exactly when the sorted content is not majorized by lambda, i.e. when there is some index k between 1 and d minus 1 for which the sum of the k largest content values exceeds the sum of the first k row lengths of lambda. Equivalently the symmetrizer leaves v nonzero precisely when the sorted content is majorized by lambda, meaning all partial sums of the sorted content are at most the corresponding partial sums of lambda. Justification: the symmetrizer ends with antisymmetrization along the columns of T, so a surviving vector must admit a placement of the multiset of labels into the diagram that is strictly increasing down every column, because any column holding two equal labels is killed by antisymmetrization. A column-strict filling of lambda using the given label multiplicities exists if and only if the sorted multiplicities fit under the row-length partial sums: seating the k most frequent labels into the diagram without a forced column repetition requires that their total count not exceed the capacity of the first k rows for every k, which is precisely the majorization condition. If this fails at some k, then the k most frequent labels cannot be seated without a repeated column entry, so every arrangement is annihilated and the symmetrizer sends v to zero.

question: For the two-dimensional unitary group, the irreducible pieces appearing in tensor powers of C^2 are indexed by partitions lambda = (lambda_1, lambda_2) with two parts. Prove that the dimension of the piece associated with such a partition equals lambda_1 minus lambda_2 plus one, and explain how this follows both from the semistandard-tableau count and from the explicit description of the piece as a determinant power times a symmetric power.
reference_answer: Semistandard count: the dimension equals the number of semistandard Young tableaux of shape lambda with entries from the two-letter alphabet {1,2}, that is fillings weakly increasing along rows and strictly increasing down columns. In the two-row shape the two cells of any column must be 1 above 2, which is forced; the only freedom is in the first row, which has lambda_1 minus lambda_2 cells beyond the part covered by the second row, and those cells must be weakly increasing in {1,2}, so they are some number of 1s followed by 2s. The number of such choices is lambda_1 minus lambda_2 plus one, giving the dimension. Explicit description: the piece is isomorphic to the determinant representation raised to the power lambda_2, tensored with the degree-m symmetric power of C^2, where m equals lambda_1 minus lambda_2. The determinant factor is one-dimensional, so it does not change the dimension; the symmetric power of degree m of a two-dimensional space has dimension m plus one. Hence the dimension is m plus one equal to lambda_1 minus lambda_2 plus one, matching the tableau count. Both routes agree because tensoring by the one-dimensional determinant shifts the highest weight without changing dimension, and the symmetric power is exactly the semistandard content of the first-row freedom.

First row, four boxes: the leftmost has three boxes to its right, two boxes below it (one in each of rows two and three in that column), plus itself, giving six; the next has two to the right, one below, plus itself, giving four; the next has one to the right, none below, plus itself, giving two; the last has none to the right, none below, plus itself, giving one. Second row, two boxes: the leftmost has one to the right, one below (row three in that column), plus itself, giving three; the next has none to the right, none below, plus itself, giving one. Third row, one box: hook length one. The product of hooks is six times four times two times one times three times one times one equal to one hundred forty-four. Then seven factorial is five thousand forty, and five thousand forty divided by one hundred forty-four equals thirty-five, so there are thirty-five standard tableaux of shape (4,2,1). Extremes: for the single row (n) every hook length is just the number of boxes to its right plus itself, giving n, n minus one, down to one, whose product is n factorial, so the count is n factorial over n factorial equal to one. For the single column with n boxes the hooks are likewise n, n minus one, down to one by symmetry, product n factorial, count one. Both extremes correctly give a single standard tableau.

question: Two permutations in the symmetric group are conjugate if and only if they have the same cycle type. Prove the key computational identity that conjugating a single cycle by an arbitrary permutation sigma relabels its entries by sigma, and use it to establish both directions of the conjugacy criterion.
reference_answer: Key identity: let a cycle send each listed entry to the next and the last back to the first, and let sigma be any permutation. The conjugate sigma times cycle times sigma inverse acts on sigma applied to a listed entry by first undoing sigma, then applying the cycle to move to the next listed entry, then applying sigma; the net effect sends sigma of an entry to sigma of the next entry, and fixes everything outside the sigma-image of the listed entries. Thus the conjugate is again a cycle of the same length whose entries are the sigma-images of the original entries. Forward direction: write any permutation as a product of disjoint cycles. Conjugating the whole product by sigma conjugates each cycle, replacing its entries by their sigma-images while preserving all cycle lengths and keeping the cycles disjoint (sigma is a bijection). Hence the conjugate has the same multiset of cycle lengths, i.e. the same cycle type. Converse: given two permutations with the same cycle type, align their disjoint-cycle decompositions so that cycles of equal length are paired, and define sigma to map the entries of each cycle of the first permutation, in order, to the entries of the paired cycle of the second. This sigma is a well-defined permutation because the cycle decompositions partition the ground set, and by the key identity it conjugates the first permutation to the second. Therefore same cycle type is equivalent to conjugacy.

question: For the second tensor power of C^d, prove that the space splits as the direct sum of the symmetric subspace and the antisymmetric subspace, that these are the plus-one and minus-one eigenspaces of the swap operator, and compute their dimensions as d times d plus one over two and d times d minus one over two respectively.
reference_answer: The swap operator F exchanges the two tensor factors; it is an involution since swapping twice is the identity, so F squared equals the identity and its eigenvalues are plus one and minus one. The operators one half times (identity plus F) and one half times (identity minus F) are complementary orthogonal projectors: they sum to the identity, each squares to itself using F squared equal to identity, and their product is zero. Their ranges are the plus-one eigenspace, the symmetric subspace of tensors unchanged by the swap, and the minus-one eigenspace, the antisymmetric subspace of tensors negated by the swap; hence the second tensor power is the direct sum of these two subspaces. Dimensions: a basis of the symmetric subspace is given by the symmetrized products of basis vectors, one for each unordered pair of indices with repetition allowed, of which there are d plus one choose two equal to d times d plus one over two. A basis of the antisymmetric subspace is given by the wedges of distinct basis vectors, one for each unordered pair of distinct indices, of which there are d choose two equal to d times d minus one over two. These dimensions sum to d squared, the dimension of the full second tensor power, confirming the direct sum.

question: Define the twirling map that averages an operator over all transformations of the form a unitary tensored with the same unitary, using the invariant measure on the unitary group. Each term of the average therefore reduces to the trace of the original state against the swap, and averaging a constant returns that constant. Hence the twirled state has the same visibility as the original.

question: A Werner state is entangled if and only if its visibility, the trace against the swap operator, is negative. Prove the entangled direction using the positive-partial-transpose criterion by computing the partial transpose of the swap operator and locating a negative eigenvalue, and explain why nonnegative visibility yields a separable state.
reference_answer: Parametrize the Werner state in the standard one-parameter family in which it is an affine combination of the identity and the swap operator with coefficients fixed by the visibility and the normalization of the trace. Partial transpose of the swap: writing the swap in a product basis as the sum over index pairs of the outer product that exchanges the two labels, transposing on the second subsystem turns it into the sum over index pairs of the outer product of a maximally correlated vector, which equals d times the projector onto the maximally entangled state. The identity is unchanged by partial transposition. Hence the partial transpose of the Werner state is an affine combination of the identity and the maximally entangled projector; this operator has two eigenvalues, one on the maximally entangled vector and one on its orthogonal complement. A short computation shows the eigenvalue associated with the maximally entangled direction is proportional to the visibility times the quantity d squared minus one, which is negative exactly when the visibility is negative (using d at least two). A state whose partial transpose has a negative eigenvalue fails the positive-partial-transpose criterion and is therefore entangled; thus negative visibility forces entanglement. Conversely, for nonnegative visibility one exhibits an explicit separable preparation: twirling a suitable product state produces a Werner state of any prescribed nonnegative visibility, and twirling preserves separability because it averages conjugates of a separable state; hence every Werner state with nonnegative visibility is separable. Combining the two directions gives the stated equivalence.

question: A multipartite state on n copies of C^d that is invariant under the simultaneous action of the same unitary on every copy must be a linear combination of the permutation operators of the symmetric group acting on the factors. By the Schur-Weyl mutual-commutant theorem these two algebras are each other's commutants inside the full operator algebra of the tensor power: the commutant of the diagonal unitary algebra is exactly the span of the factor permutations. The invariance hypothesis states that conjugating the state by every diagonal unitary leaves it fixed, which is equivalent to the state commuting with every diagonal unitary (conjugation invariance for unitaries is the same as commuting with them). Therefore the state lies in the commutant of the diagonal unitary algebra. By the mutual-commutant theorem that commutant is the span of the factor permutations, so the state is a linear combination of the permutation operators, as claimed. The remark that these permutation operators are not in general positive semidefinite shows this expansion, while always valid, need not display the state as a manifestly valid density operator; that is a separate positivity question, not an obstruction to the linear-combination conclusion.

question: A permutation-invariant operator on the n-fold tensor power of C^d, meaning one unchanged by conjugation by every factor permutation, is determined by only polynomially many parameters in n when d is held fixed. Explain precisely why, using the Schur-Weyl block decomposition together with the polynomial bounds on the number of diagrams and on the dimensions of the unitary-group pieces.
reference_answer: By Schur-Weyl duality the tensor power decomposes into blocks indexed by Young diagrams with at most d rows, each block a tensor product of a symmetric-group piece and a unitary-group piece. Permutation invariance, via the mutual-commutant structure, forces the operator to act as the identity on each symmetric-group factor and to be an arbitrary operator on each unitary-group factor; concretely the operator is a direct sum over diagrams of the identity on the symmetric-group piece tensored with a free operator on the unitary-group piece. The number of free parameters is therefore the sum over admissible diagrams of the squared dimension of the unitary-group piece. Two polynomial bounds control this. First, the number of admissible diagrams is at most the number of ways to fill d row lengths each between zero and n, bounded by n plus one to the power d, which is polynomial in n for fixed d. Second, the dimension of each unitary-group piece is bounded by a fixed polynomial in n of degree depending only on d, namely at most n plus one to the power d times d minus one over two. Multiplying a polynomial number of diagrams by a polynomial squared dimension gives a total parameter count polynomial in n with d fixed. Hence a permutation-invariant operator, though living in an exponentially large space, is pinned down by only polynomially many numbers.

question: Let a density operator on C^d have spectrum given by a probability vector in non-increasing order, and consider the n-fold tensor power of this density operator decomposed by Schur-Weyl into blocks indexed by Young diagrams. reference_answer: The tensor power of the density operator is permutation invariant, so by Schur-Weyl it is block diagonal with one block per admissible diagram; the weight of a block is the trace of the tensor power restricted to that block. This weight factorizes as the dimension of the symmetric-group piece times the trace of the induced operator on the unitary-group piece. Writing the normalized diagram as the row-length vector divided by n, the two-sided bound on this weight is governed by the relative entropy between the normalized diagram and the spectrum: up to polynomial-in-n prefactors, the weight is the exponential of minus n times the relative entropy of the normalized diagram against the spectrum. Relative entropy is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when the normalized diagram equals the spectrum. Therefore when the normalized diagram is far from the spectrum the relative entropy is bounded away from zero and the weight decays exponentially in n; only diagrams whose normalized row lengths are close to the spectrum, where the relative entropy is near zero, retain non-negligible weight. The polynomial prefactors, coming from the number of diagrams and the dimension bounds, cannot overcome the exponential suppression, so for large n the probability mass concentrates on normalized diagrams near the spectrum. The exact decay rate is the relative entropy of the normalized diagram against the spectrum, appearing in the exponent multiplied by minus n.

question: A bipartite state of equal local dimension is called isotropic if it is invariant under conjugation by every transformation of the form a unitary tensored with its complex conjugate. Prove that a state is isotropic if and only if its partial transpose on the second subsystem is a Werner state, using the algebraic identity relating partial transposition to conjugation by a unitary and its conjugate.
reference_answer: Recall the identity for partial transposition on the second subsystem: for operators X_1, Y_1, X_2, Y_2 and any middle operator Z, the partial transpose of (X_1 tensor Y_1) Z (X_2 tensor Y_2) equals (X_1 tensor the transpose of Y_2) times the partial transpose of Z times (X_2 tensor the transpose of Y_1). Apply this with the isotropic symmetry transformation, namely X_1 = X_2 = a unitary and Y_1 = Y_2 = its complex conjugate, acting on the state. On the left we partial-transpose the conjugated state; using that the transpose of the complex conjugate of a unitary is its adjoint, the right side becomes the unitary tensored with the unitary (not its conjugate) acting by conjugation on the partial transpose of the state. Therefore: the state is unchanged by conjugation with a unitary tensored with its conjugate if and only if, after partial transposition, the partial transpose is unchanged by conjugation with a unitary tensored with the same unitary. The former is exactly the isotropic symmetry; the latter is exactly the Werner symmetry. Hence a state is isotropic precisely when its partial transpose on the second subsystem is a Werner state. question: Fix a total space of dimension 2 and a system embedding that sends the single system index to total index 0, so the clean block is the one entry U(0,0). A contributor claims that specifying the target A (here the scalar at position (0,0)) and demanding U be real orthogonal determines U uniquely. Refute this: for the target entry x with 0 < |x| < 1, exhibit two DISTINCT real orthogonal 2x2 matrices whose clean block is the same x, verify both are orthogonal, identify exactly which matrix data is left free by the block-encoding contract, and state the general principle about how much of U a clean-block (or even clean-action) certificate pins down.
reference_answer: The clean block under this embedding is the single entry U(0,0); the contract only requires U(0,0) = x (times the normalizer, here 1) and U real orthogonal. Two distinct witnesses with x in (0,1), set s = sqrt(1-x^2) > 0: U1 = [[x, -s],[s, x]] (a proper rotation) and U2 = [[x, s],[s, -x]] (a reflection). Both have clean block U1(0,0) = U2(0,0) = x. Orthogonality: U1 columns have squared norms x^2+s^2 = 1 and x^2+s^2 = 1 with cross term x*(-s)+s*x = 0; U2 columns have x^2+s^2 = 1 and s^2+x^2 = 1 with cross term x*s + s*(-x) = 0. So both are orthogonal, and U1 != U2 because their (0,1) entries are -s and s and their (1,1) entries are x and -x (and s > 0). Hence the target entry plus orthogonality does NOT determine U: the block-encoding contract constrains only the clean (embedded) rows and columns, and everything off that clean embedding - the 'garbage' or failure branch - is free, subject only to making the whole matrix orthogonal. General principle: a clean-block certificate fixes U exactly on the clean sub-block (the all-zero-ancilla rows and columns); the orthogonal complement (the nonzero-ancilla branch) is determined only up to any completion to a unitary, so infinitely many distinct U (for larger blocks) share the same block encoding of A. Even the stronger clean-ACTION certificate (U on every clean basis input, read on clean outputs) pins only the clean block and the same freedom remains, because that action and the clean block carry identical information. The practical consequence: you cannot read U, its depth, or its ancilla content off A alone; distinct constructions with very different costs can encode the same A, which is exactly why the benchmark certifies clean blocks and charges resources separately rather than treating the dilating unitary as unique.

question: A logical linear-combination-of-unitaries block encoding is assembled as unprepare after select after amplitude after prepare, on a product of a coefficient register, a selector register, and the system register. Describe the role of each of the four stages, say which registers each stage touches, and explain why the final stage is the adjoint (dagger) of the first rather than an independent gate. What exactly plays the role of the ancilla that must be returned to zero?
reference_answer: PREPARE acts on the selector register (lifted by tensoring with identities on the coefficient and system registers): it loads the superposition of selector values whose amplitudes encode the LCU weights. AMPLITUDE is a selector- and system-controlled family of unitaries acting on the coefficient register (block-diagonal over the (selector,system) context): it writes the per-term coefficient/rotation into the coefficient register. SELECT is a basis permutation that applies, controlled by the selector value, the chosen system permutation to the system register while preserving coefficient and selector: it applies the term unitaries to the data. UNPREPARE is the adjoint of PREPARE on the selector register; it must be the dagger of the first stage because the clean block is read by projecting the selector (and coefficient) back onto the clean value, and only PREPARE-dagger coherently recombines the selector superposition so the surviving clean amplitude is the weighted sum of term contributions. An independent gate would not guarantee that the clean projection reconstructs the intended weights or returns the selector to zero. The ancilla that must return to zero is the selector register (together with the coefficient register pinned to its clean value); PREPARE and UNPREPARE act on this SAME selector register, which is what produces the weight structure in the clean entry.

question: Fix the clean signal value. Prove that the following two certificate conditions are equivalent: (i) the projected system x system block of U equals a target A entrywise; (ii) for every system basis input and output, the clean output amplitude of U on the clean basis input (clean signal, basis input) equals A(output,input). Explain each direction, name the single linear-algebra fact that makes one clean-basis amplitude equal to one projected-block entry, and state how (ii) extends from basis inputs to an arbitrary normalized system input.
reference_answer: Write the compound (flattened) index for signal value s and system index k as s*systemDim + k, with s fixed to the clean value throughout. The projected block entry at (output,input) is block(output,input) = U(clean*systemDim+output, clean*systemDim+input). The clean output amplitude is the coordinate at compound index (clean,output) of the vector U applied to the basis ket at compound index (clean,input). Key fact: applying a matrix to a computational basis ket selects the corresponding column of the matrix (mulVec of a single-one indicator yields that column). Hence the clean output amplitude equals U(clean*systemDim+output, clean*systemDim+input), which is exactly block(output,input). (i) => (ii): if block = A entrywise, then for each (output,input) the clean output amplitude equals block(output,input) = A(output,input). (ii) => (i): if every clean output amplitude equals A(output,input), then by the same column-selection identity every projected-block entry equals A(output,input), so block = A entrywise. The two statements are therefore pointwise equivalent at the fixed signal value. Extension to arbitrary input: write a normalized system state as a linear combination of system basis vectors; the clean output on this input is the same linear combination of the per-basis clean outputs by linearity of matrix-vector action, so the clean-branch action equals A acting on the system state (up to the normalizer and the orthogonal failure branch, which only records the unitarity probability deficit). This equivalence is why a construction may prove the block directly or prove the clean action and conclude the other.

question: For the logical unprepare-select-amplitude-prepare LCU matrix on registers coefficient x (selector x system), derive the exact clean projected entry between clean input (clean coefficient, clean selector, systemColumn) and clean output (clean coefficient, clean selector, systemRow). Show that it is a finite sum over selector indices, that each surviving term carries the SELECT matching condition on the system permutation, and that each term's weight is the conjugate of a PREPARE amplitude times the controlled coefficient rotation diagonal entry times the PREPARE amplitude. reference_answer: Project the logical matrix onto the clean coefficient and clean selector on both sides, leaving system indices systemRow (output) and systemColumn (input). The clean entry equals the finite sum over all selector indices j of: [if permutation(j) applied to systemColumn equals systemRow then conj(prepare(j, cleanSelector)) * rotation(j, systemColumn)(cleanCoefficient, cleanCoefficient) * prepare(j, cleanSelector) else 0]. Derivation: UNPREPARE = PREPARE-dagger lifted on the selector contributes the clean bra, which turns the matrix product into a selector sum against conj(prepare(j, cleanSelector)) and forces the coefficient and system row labels; AMPLITUDE contributes the controlled coefficient-register entry rotation(j, systemColumn)(cleanCoefficient, cleanCoefficient) on the clean coefficient diagonal; SELECT contributes the indicator that the controlled system permutation for selector j maps the input systemColumn to the output systemRow; PREPARE contributes the ket amplitude prepare(j, cleanSelector). The selector weight is conj(prepare(j,cleanSelector)) * (...) * prepare(j,cleanSelector): the factor prepare(j,cleanSelector) comes from PREPARE loading the selector superposition from the clean selector, and the factor conj(prepare(j,cleanSelector)) comes from UNPREPARE = PREPARE-dagger projecting back onto the clean selector. Physically this is why PREPARE and UNPREPARE must be the SAME gate up to adjoint acting on the SAME selector register: the clean amplitude of each term is weighted by |prepare(j,cleanSelector)|^2 when the coefficient rotation diagonal is 1, i.e. by the probability of selecting term j, so the clean block is the probability-weighted (and coefficient-weighted) combination of the per-term system permutations. If prepare and unprepare were independent, the two factors would not form conj(x)*x and the clean weights would not be the intended squared selection amplitudes.

question: A block encoding is read by preparing the auxiliary register in the all-zero state, applying U, and postselecting the auxiliary register back on all-zero. Suppose U block-encodes A with normalizer alpha (so the auxiliary-zero projected block equals A/alpha) and the input system state is a normalized vector v. Express the unnormalized clean output branch and its squared norm, give the exact success probability of the all-zero postselection, and state when this probability equals (||A v|| / alpha)^2. Why is the success probability generally strictly below 1, and what does this cost imply for using the block encoding as a subroutine?
reference_answer: Prepare |0^a> tensor |v>, apply U. Decompose the output as |0^a> tensor w_clean + (orthogonal auxiliary-nonzero branches), where w_clean = (<0^a| tensor I) U (|0^a> tensor |v>). Because the auxiliary-zero projected block of U equals A/alpha, w_clean = (A/alpha) v. The all-zero postselection keeps exactly the clean branch, so the unnormalized clean output is (A/alpha) v with squared norm ||(A/alpha) v||^2 = ||A v||^2 / alpha^2, and the post-measurement normalized state is (A v)/||A v||. The success probability of the all-zero auxiliary outcome is therefore p = ||A v||^2 / alpha^2 = (||A v|| / alpha)^2. This equals (||A v||/alpha)^2 exactly whenever the projected block is exactly A/alpha (the exact block-encoding case); in the epsilon-approximate case it is this value up to an O(epsilon) correction. Since U is unitary, the total output norm is 1, so p <= 1 with equality only in the degenerate case ||A v|| = alpha (e.g. alpha = ||A|| and v a top singular vector with the orthogonal branch empty); generically ||A v|| < alpha (alpha is chosen at least the operator norm so the encoding is valid for all v), so p < 1 strictly. The cost implication: one query to U succeeds with probability p that can be far below 1, so naive repetition costs O(1/p) = O(alpha^2/||A v||^2) trials; amplitude amplification reduces this to O(alpha/||A v||) queries. This 1/alpha success penalty is exactly why the normalizer alpha is a charged resource and why alpha should be kept close to ||A||.

question: Consider the 2x2 scalar dilation whose top-left clean entry is x, whose two off-diagonal entries are both y, and whose bottom-right entry is -x. Treat the single top-left entry as the one-dimensional clean block encoding the scalar x with normalizer 1. Determine the exact condition on (x,y) under which this dilation is orthogonal (a valid real one-qubit-signal block encoding), compute the two row self-overlaps and the row cross-overlap, and explain the boundary: what is the largest |x| for which a real y exists making the dilation orthogonal, and what does exceeding it mean for block-encoding a scalar of magnitude greater than 1 with normalizer 1?
reference_answer: The dilation matrix is [[x, y],[y, -x]]. Its row self-overlaps are: row 0 with itself = x*x + y*y, row 1 with itself = (-x)*(-x) + y*y = x*x + y*y, and the row cross-overlap (row 0 with row 1) = x*y + y*(-x) = x*y - x*y = 0. So the rows are automatically orthogonal to each other for all (x,y), and the matrix is orthogonal (a valid real block encoding whose clean block is the scalar x) exactly when the common self-overlap equals 1, i.e. x*x + y*y = 1. Given x, a real y with y*y = 1 - x*x exists iff 1 - x*x >= 0, i.e. |x| <= 1; then y = +/- sqrt(1 - x^2). The largest |x| admitting a real y is therefore |x| = 1 (at which y = 0 and the dilation is diag(1,-1) up to sign). Boundary meaning: a 1x1 clean block with normalizer 1 can only encode a scalar of magnitude at most 1; this is the contraction constraint, since the clean block of any unitary (or orthogonal) matrix is a contraction with operator norm at most 1. To block-encode a scalar c with |c| > 1 one must either raise the normalizer to alpha >= |c| (encoding c/alpha, which again has magnitude <= 1) or use a larger signal register; no choice of real y rescues |x| > 1. Thus the scalar-dilation gives the sharp one-dimensional instance of the general lower bound: the encoded block, before dividing by the normalizer, cannot have norm exceeding 1.

reference_answer: The one-sparse model is: oneSparseMatrix c amp has entry (row,col) = amp(col) if row = c(col), else 0 - so each column has its single possible nonzero at the single row c(col). The reconstruction lemma assumes the target is supported only at row = c(col), i.e. for all row != c(col), target(row,col) = 0 (one nonzero per column at a FIXED location). Counterexample to the overbroad claim: take the 2x2 target A with A(0,0)=1, A(1,0)=1, and column 1 all zero. Column 0 has TWO nonzeros (rows 0 and 1), so there is no single support value c(0) with target(row,0)=0 for all row != c(0): whichever of row 0 or 1 we pick as c(0), the other row is a nonzero off-support entry. Hence the support hypothesis fails and oneSparseMatrix c (fun col => A (c col) col) cannot equal A for any c: it would zero out one of the two entries. The violated hypothesis is precisely 'row != c(col) implies target(row,col)=0'. Now a genuine zero-containing one-sparse target that IS reconstructed: take B 2x2 with B(0,0)=0 (column 0 entirely zero) and B(1,1)=3 (column 1 nonzero at row 1), all other entries 0. Choose c(0)=0 and c(1)=1. For column 0, amp(0)=B(c(0),0)=B(0,0)=0, and every entry is 0, matching B; the zero amplitude is allowed. For column 1, amp(1)=B(1,1)=3 at row 1 and 0 elsewhere, matching B. So oneSparseMatrix c amp = B exactly. Conclusion: one nonzero per column at a fixed support location (including the degenerate zero-amplitude column) is fine; TWO nonzeros in a column breaks the sole hypothesis and is a true counterexample to the overbroad claim.

reference_answer: The assembly adds three scaled sources (each scaled by 1/2): a controlled-phase source for A with filler phase, one for A-dagger with filler phase, and a Pauli-X-tensor-B term that has zero lower-right block. The lower-right filler of a scaled controlled-phase source with normalizer N and phase e^{i*phi} is (1/2)*N*e^{i*phi} on the diagonal. With BOTH A and A-dagger terms using phase e^{i*pi} = -1, the lower-right diagonal clean entry is (1/2)*N*(-1) + (1/2)*N*(-1) + 0 = -N. So the printed clean lower-right block equals -N (the identity-filler blocks ADD rather than cancel). But the intended Hermitian piece S1 has lower-right block equal to 0 (S1 is the Hermitian part of the homogenized matrix [[A,B],[0,0]], whose lower-right block is 0). Therefore, if N != 0, the printed clean block has lower-right entry -N != 0 = S1's lower-right entry, so the printed-phase clean block is NOT equal to S1 - a genuine counterexample to the all-(-1) cancellation claim. Corrected assignment: give the two filler phases OPPOSITE signs, e.g. keep the A-dagger term at phase -1 but set the A term's filler phase to 0 (i.e. e^{i*0}=+1) while leaving its upper operator block intact. Then the lower-right clean entry becomes (1/2)*N*(+1) + (1/2)*N*(-1) + 0 = 0, matching S1's zero lower-right block, and the upper A, A-dagger and off-diagonal B blocks are unchanged, so the phase-balanced clean block equals S1 exactly (under the paper's Hermitian B). question: A reversible-classical block-encoding route realizes the full unitary as a permutation matrix on the flattened ancilla-system basis, with the clean block taken from the all-zero ancilla embedding. Prove that a permutation matrix built from a bijective index map is a valid real orthogonal unitary proxy (its column and row Gram matrices are the identity), and separately give the exact clean-block entry formula for such a permutation under the product embedding. Explain why bijectivity (not merely injectivity) is needed for the row Gram condition, and why the clean block of a permutation is itself a 0/1 partial-permutation matrix rather than an arbitrary target.
reference_answer: A permutation matrix for an index map p has entry (row,col) = 1 if row = p(col) else 0. Column Gram: columnInner(i,j) = sum over k of permMatrix(k,i)*permMatrix(k,j). The product permMatrix(k,i)*permMatrix(k,j) is nonzero only when k = p(i) and k = p(j) simultaneously. If i = j the unique surviving term is at k = p(i) giving 1; if i != j then p(i) != p(j) by INJECTIVITY, so no k satisfies both and the sum is 0. Hence columnInner = identity using only injectivity. Row Gram: rowInner(i,j) = sum over k of permMatrix(i,k)*permMatrix(j,k), nonzero only when i = p(k) and j = p(k). For the diagonal i = j we need SOME k with p(k) = i, i.e. i is in the image of p; this requires SURJECTIVITY. With bijectivity, for each i there is exactly one such k (hit = p^{-1}(i)) giving 1, and for i != j no k maps to both, giving 0, so rowInner = identity. Thus bijectivity (injective AND surjective) yields IsRationalOrthogonal(permMatrix p): injectivity alone secures the column condition, but the row (diagonal) condition can fail without surjectivity because some row might have no preimage and give rowInner(i,i)=0 != 1. Clean block entry: under the product embedding productIndex (ancilla, system) mapping (a,s) to a*system + s, the clean block uses the all-zero ancilla embedding, and cleanBlockProduct(zero, permMatrix p)(row,col) = 1 if productIndex(zero,row) = p(productIndex(zero,col)) else 0. This is manifestly a 0/1 matrix with at most one 1 per column (a partial permutation of the system basis): it can only equal targets that are themselves 0/1 partial permutations, so a permutation-matrix block encoding cannot directly encode a target with non-0/1 entries - that needs weighting/LCU layers on top. The reversible-classical route therefore certifies exactly the partial-permutation clean blocks and no more.

reference_answer: An exact clean-block certificate carries: a full matrix U on the total (ancilla+system) basis, a target system-space matrix A, an embedding of the system basis into the total basis, and a proof that the embedded clean block of U equals A pointwise (the clean submatrix equals A entry by entry). The zero-error promotion sets epsilon = 0 and sets the approximation predicate to be exactly that same pointwise clean-block equality, with the approximation proof being the certificate's own block proof. This is legitimate because the approximate incumbent's bound field is a PROPOSITION that different backends may instantiate; the exact finite route instantiates the epsilon=0 bound by the exact pointwise equality it already proved, so no analytic operator-norm reasoning is introduced - the promotion is a repackaging, not a new theorem. Boundary the other way: holding this zero-error approximate incumbent does NOT by itself yield the analytic statement ||A - alpha*block|| <= 0 in an operator-norm sense. The finite certificate proves ENTRYWISE (pointwise) equality of the clean block with A/normalizer; converting that to an operator-norm inequality (or to the statement that the operator-norm distance is 0) requires the extra ingredient of a theorem connecting pointwise/entrywise equality of finite matrices to the chosen matrix norm (e.g. that pointwise equality implies equality as operators and hence zero norm difference). The source is explicit that analytic backends can LATER replace the exact-as-approximate packaging with such a theorem; until then the epsilon=0 incumbent is a faithful exact-equality witness, not an analytic norm certificate. reference_answer: If the control predicate is false, the gate leaves the whole bit string unchanged, so a second application also does nothing. question: Let S and T be Hermitian matrices on one finite system and X a Hermitian matrix on a second system. Prove that H=S tensor X+T tensor I is Hermitian without assuming that S and T commute. Give a counterexample showing that the same conclusion can fail if X is not Hermitian.
reference_answer: The adjoint of a tensor product is the tensor product of the adjoints: entrywise, conjugating S(j,i)X(v,u) gives S(i,j)X(u,v) under Hermiticity of both factors. Hence (S tensor X) dagger=S tensor X. Similarly T tensor I is Hermitian because I dagger=I. Adjoint is additive, so H dagger=H. No product S T occurs anywhere in this argument, so S and T need not commute. The premise on X matters: take the first system one-dimensional with S=[1], T=[0], and X=[[0,1],[0,0]]. Then H=X, whereas X dagger=[[0,0],[1,0]] is different. This is an operator-algebra closure result, not a claim that implementing the factors or reading out a simulated evolution is free.

question: A finite row stencil is a list of offset/coefficient pairs. Its matrix entry at row i and column j is the sum of coefficients of every pair with i+offset=j; no modular wrapping is used. Prove that merging repeated offsets by summing their coefficients leaves every matrix entry unchanged. reference_answer: Fix i,j. Every pair contributes its coefficient if its offset equals j-i and contributes zero otherwise. Group the finite sum by equal offsets; associativity and commutativity of scalar addition preserve the sum. Replacing each group by a single pair whose coefficient is that group sum therefore gives exactly the same entry for this arbitrary i,j, hence the same matrix. In the example the offset1 coefficient is2-2=0, while the offset-1 coefficient is3. Thus the entry at j=i+1 vanishes and the entry at j=i-1 equals3 if that column lies in the finite grid. The original list has three pairs, its merged list can have two pairs including a zero, and it has at most one nonzero matrix entry in a row; at a left boundary even that entry may disappear because j=i-1 is outside the grid. An access permutation or sparse-oracle cost cannot be inferred solely from the unmerged list length. This proof uses the stated additive matrix semantics, not a claim that arbitrary loaders with collided labels are automatically reversible.

question: A single core of a finite real tensor train is a real matrix whose rows are indexed by the left bond and whose columns are indexed by a composite label: an ordered pair of an emitted bit (two values) and a right-bond index (r values). To factorize this core, one reshapes that composite column label into a single flat column label and then performs a thin factorization in the flat coordinates. Explain (a) why the reshaping is a genuine bijection and what the flat label's size is, (b) why performing the factorization in flat coordinates and then relabeling the result back by the inverse reshaping produces valid factors of the original core, and (c) why the row-orthonormality of the orthonormal factor is unaffected by the relabeling. State the resulting inner (new left-bond) dimension.
reference_answer: (a) The composite column label ranges over all ordered pairs (bit, right-bond index) with the bit taking 2 values and the right-bond index taking r values. The set of such pairs has exactly 2 times r elements, and there is a fixed bijection between it and the flat label set {0,...,2r-1}; reshaping is simply applying this bijection, so no column is lost, duplicated, or merged. The flat label therefore has size 2r. (b) A thin factorization in flat coordinates writes the reshaped core as R times Q where Q has orthonormal rows. Relabeling the columns of Q back by the inverse bijection permutes/renames columns without changing any entry, so the matrix product R times (relabeled Q) reproduces the original core entry by entry: for each original column (bit, j) the entry equals the flat-coordinate entry at the image label, which the factorization already matches. Hence R and the relabeled Q are valid factors of the original core. (c) Row-orthonormality is the statement that Q times Q-transpose equals the identity, i.e. each pair of rows has the prescribed inner product summed over columns. Relabeling columns by a bijection only reorders the terms of that per-row-pair sum, and a finite sum is invariant under reindexing by a bijection, so the row-Gram matrix is unchanged; the relabeled Q still has orthonormal rows. The inner (new left-bond) dimension is the minimum of the original left bond and 2r, i.e. min(left bond, 2 * right bond).

question: During backward canonicalization of a finite real tensor train, a residual matrix R (left over from factorizing a later core) must be absorbed into the right bond of the preceding core A, where A emits one bit of two possible values and has a right-bond index. The absorption produces a new core whose entry at left index a and composite column (bit, j) is the sum over the old right-bond index b of A at (a, bit, b) times R at (b, j). Explain in matrix-slice terms what this absorption does to each of the two emitted-bit branches of A, and justify why it does not mix the two bit branches together. State the single slice identity that captures this.
reference_answer: View the core A, with the emitted bit fixed to a value, as an ordinary matrix called the bit-slice of A for that bit value: its rows are indexed by the left bond and its columns by the right bond. The absorption of R multiplies each such bit-slice on the right by R: the bit-value-0 slice of the absorbed core is the bit-value-0 slice of A times R, and the bit-value-1 slice of the absorbed core is the bit-value-1 slice of A times R. In other words absorption is just an independent right matrix multiplication performed within each emitted-bit branch. It cannot mix the two branches because the defining sum runs only over the old right-bond index b and carries the emitted bit through unchanged on both sides: the bit label of an output column equals the bit label fed in, and R acts only on the right-bond coordinate, never on the bit coordinate. The single identity that captures this is: the bit-b slice of (absorb A R) equals (the bit-b slice of A) times R, for each bit value b. This is why absorption changes bond dimensions on the right while preserving the bit structure the core emits.

question: A stencil coefficient is written in a small symbolic language whose expressions are built from rational constants, named symbols, and the operations addition, multiplication, and negation. Given an environment that assigns a rational number to each symbol name, the coefficient is turned into a concrete rational number by a single evaluation map. State how this map treats each of the five kinds of expression, and state precisely which algebraic structure the evaluation preserves (that is, which equalities relate the value of a compound expression to the values of its parts).
reference_answer: Evaluation sends a rational-constant expression to that same rational number; it sends a symbol to whatever rational the environment assigns to that symbol's name; and it is defined recursively on the three operations so that the value of a sum is the sum of the values, the value of a product is the product of the values, and the value of a negation is the negation of the value. In other words, for a fixed environment the evaluation map is a homomorphism of the symbolic coefficient algebra onto the rationals: it commutes with addition, with multiplication, and with negation, and it maps the constant symbols for 0 and 1 to the rationals 0 and 1. Consequently any symbolic identity built only from +, *, and negation holds for the evaluated rationals, which is exactly what lets symbolic stencil rows be manipulated before any numeric assignment is chosen.

question: You are given r real column vectors in R^N that are orthonormal (each has unit length and distinct ones are orthogonal), presented as the columns of an N-by-r matrix V satisfying V-transpose times V equals the r-by-r identity. You are also given an arbitrary assignment that places these r columns into r distinct column positions among the N columns of a target N-by-N matrix (the positions need not be the first r columns, and need not be contiguous). Prove that there exists an N-by-N real orthogonal matrix U (U-transpose times U equals the N-by-N identity) whose columns at exactly those r prescribed positions are the given vectors. Make explicit each ingredient your argument relies on.
reference_answer: First, the hypothesis V-transpose times V = identity says exactly that the r columns of V form an orthonormal family of vectors in R^N; in particular the family has r elements and since an orthonormal family is linearly independent, r <= N. Second, the prescribed placement is an injection from the r column-labels into the N positions, so it merely relabels the same r orthonormal vectors at distinct physical positions without changing their inner products; the placed family is therefore still orthonormal. Third, in the N-dimensional inner-product space R^N, any orthonormal family can be extended to an orthonormal basis of the whole space (basis-extension / Gram-Schmidt completion); this produces N - r additional unit vectors orthogonal to each other and to the prescribed ones, filling the N - r unused positions. Fourth, assemble U by taking as its columns these N orthonormal vectors, with the prescribed vectors sitting at their assigned positions and the completion vectors at the remaining positions. Because all N columns are orthonormal, U-transpose times U is the identity, i.e. U is orthogonal, and by construction its columns at the prescribed positions are exactly the given vectors. Hence such a U exists. The essential ingredients are: (i) the equivalence between the identity equation and column-orthonormality, (ii) invariance of orthonormality under an injective relabeling of positions, and (iii) the orthonormal-basis extension theorem in a finite-dimensional inner-product space whose dimension equals the number of positions.

question: Suppose r orthonormal real columns are placed at r distinct positions among the N columns of an orthogonal matrix, and suppose r < N so at least one column position is left free. The naive completion to an orthogonal matrix may land in the reflection family (determinant -1) rather than the rotation family (determinant +1). Prove that one can always repair the orientation so the final matrix has determinant exactly +1 while leaving every one of the r prescribed columns completely unchanged. Explain why the strict inequality r < N is exactly what makes the repair possible, and why the repair cannot in general be done when r = N.
reference_answer: Start from any orthogonal completion U whose prescribed columns are the given vectors. Because U is orthogonal, U-transpose U = I forces det(U)^2 = 1, so det(U) is either +1 or -1. If it is already +1 there is nothing to do. If it is -1, we fix it with a single-column sign flip at an unused position. Since r < N, the r prescribed positions do not exhaust the N columns, so there is at least one position, call it 'unused', that carries no prescribed column. Let S be the diagonal matrix that is the identity except for a -1 in the unused position. S is orthogonal (it is diagonal with entries +/-1, so S-transpose S = I) and det(S) = -1. Replace U by U*S. Then (U S)-transpose (U S) = S-transpose (U-transpose U) S = S-transpose S = I, so U*S is still orthogonal; and det(U S) = det(U) det(S) = (-1)(-1) = +1, so it is now a rotation. Crucially, right-multiplying by this diagonal S only rescales the single unused column by -1 and leaves every other column, in particular all r prescribed columns, exactly as it was. Hence the prescribed data is preserved and the orientation is corrected. The strict inequality r < N is essential because the repair needs a column that is NOT prescribed to absorb the sign flip; if r = N every column is prescribed, flipping any of them would change the required data, and indeed a fully prescribed orthonormal frame with determinant -1 simply cannot be reoriented to +1 without altering a prescribed column, so no determinant-+1 completion that fixes all N columns exists.

question: In a finite complex matrix backend, acting with an operator on a computational-basis state (a vector with a single 1 at one position and 0 elsewhere) returns the corresponding column of the operator. Using only this fact and the linearity of matrix-vector multiplication, prove that acting with an operator A on the two-term superposition a*|left> + b*|right>, where |left> and |right> are two basis states, gives a*(column left of A) + b*(column right of A), and that the amplitude read at output row k equals a*A[k,left] + b*A[k,right]. Explain why this means a block-encoding or state-preparation witness never needs to reconstruct the whole matrix-vector product: only two named columns, or two named entries, are ever required.
reference_answer: Matrix-vector multiplication is linear in the vector argument: for scalars a, b and vectors u, w we have A(a*u + b*w) = a*(A u) + b*(A w), and A(c*u) = c*(A u). Apply this with u = |left> and w = |right>. By the basis-column fact, A|left> is exactly the 'left' column of A and A|right> is exactly the 'right' column of A. Therefore A(a*|left> + b*|right>) = a*(A|left>) + b*(A|right>) = a*(column left of A) + b*(column right of A). Reading the k-th coordinate of both sides and using that the k-th coordinate of the 'j' column of A is the entry A[k,j], the output amplitude at row k is a*A[k,left] + b*A[k,right]. Consequently, to certify what an operator does to any two-term superposition it suffices to inspect the two named columns (vector form) or, for a single output amplitude, just the two named matrix entries (scalar form). No sum over all basis states or full reconstruction of the matrix-vector product is needed; the sparsity of the input collapses the computation to exactly the terms whose input amplitude is nonzero. This is why finite preparation and block-encoding witnesses are stated and checked column-wise or entry-wise rather than by rebuilding a dense product.

question: Two proof styles are commonly used to certify that a flattened signal-system unitary block-encodes a target operator on the system register at a fixed 'clean' signal value. Style A proves a pointwise equality: the matrix block obtained by projecting the unitary onto that clean signal branch equals the target matrix entry by entry. Style B proves an action statement: for every clean-signal basis input and every clean-signal output row, the amplitude the unitary produces equals the corresponding target matrix entry. Prove that these two styles are logically equivalent, by first showing the single bridging identity that the clean-input/clean-output amplitude of the unitary equals exactly one entry of the projected block.
reference_answer: The bridge is: for a fixed clean signal value and any output and input system indices, the amplitude obtained by feeding the clean-signal basis input into the unitary and reading the clean-signal output row equals exactly the (output, input) entry of the projected block of the unitary at that signal value. This holds because acting on a basis ket selects a column (the basis-column fact), and selecting the clean-output coordinate of that column is by definition the same entry that the signal-branch projection reads off; so the amplitude and the projected-block entry are literally the same number for every output and input. Now prove the equivalence. (Style A implies Style B) Assume the projected block equals the target entrywise. Fix any output and input. By the bridge the clean-input/clean-output amplitude equals the projected-block (output,input) entry, which by assumption equals the target (output,input) entry; so the action statement holds for every output and input. (Style B implies Style A) Assume the action statement holds for all outputs and inputs. Fix any output and input; the projected-block (output,input) entry equals, by the bridge, the clean-input/clean-output amplitude, which by assumption equals the target (output,input) entry; so the projected block equals the target entrywise. Since each direction follows from the single bridging identity applied at an arbitrary (output, input) pair, the two certification styles are equivalent. (Linearity further extends the basis action to arbitrary system inputs, and any orthogonal failure branch is separate unitarity evidence rather than a competing block contract.)

question: Let V be a real N-by-r matrix whose columns are orthonormal, expressed by the identity V-transpose times V equals the r-by-r identity. (a) Prove the dimensional obstruction r <= N. (b) Suppose further that the strict inequality r < N holds and that the r columns are placed at r distinct positions among the N available column positions via an injective assignment from the r column-labels into the N positions. Prove that this assignment cannot be surjective, i.e. at least one of the N positions receives no prescribed column. Make the counting argument explicit and explain how these two facts together guarantee a spare position exists exactly when r < N.
reference_answer: (a) The identity V-transpose times V = identity says that for every pair of column labels the inner product of the corresponding columns is 1 when the labels agree and 0 when they differ; that is, the r columns form an orthonormal family in R^N. An orthonormal family is linearly independent: if a linear combination of the columns were zero, taking the inner product with each column in turn (using orthonormality) forces every coefficient to be zero. A linearly independent family in an N-dimensional vector space has at most N members, because its size cannot exceed the dimension. Hence r, the number of columns, satisfies r <= N. This is the isometry dimensional obstruction: an inner-product-preserving (isometric) linear map from R^r into R^N can exist only when r <= N. (b) The placement is an injective function e from the r column-labels into the N positions. Suppose, for contradiction, that e were also surjective. A surjection from a finite set of size r onto a finite set of size N forces the size of the target to be at most the size of the source, i.e. N <= r (a surjection cannot increase cardinality). But we assumed r < N, i.e. N > r, contradicting N <= r. Therefore e is not surjective: there exists at least one position in the N positions that is not in the image of e, i.e. an unused position receiving no prescribed column. Together: part (a) shows orthonormal columns can only exist when r <= N, and part (b) shows that in the strict regime r < N the injective placement always leaves a spare position. When instead r = N, the injection is a bijection and no spare position exists, which is precisely the boundary that distinguishes the two regimes.

question: When embedding a right-canonical tensor-train core into a larger fixed physical register by zero-padding its outputs, one claims the active clean-input columns remain orthonormal and that right-multiplication of the boundary stays mass-preserving. A reviewer argues: 'the padded core still satisfies core times core-transpose equals the identity on the physical register, so its rows are orthonormal and nothing changes'. Show by an explicit small example that the reviewer's blanket claim is false: padding generally destroys the ROW orthonormality relation even though it preserves the COLUMN orthonormality of the active clean-input columns. State precisely which relation survives padding and which does not, and why only the surviving one is used.
reference_answer: Take the simplest nontrivial case: a core whose matrix, after fixing the emitted bit, acts as the 1-by-1 identity (its single active row/column is the scalar 1), and pad its output into a physical register of dimension 2 by appending a zero output row. Writing the padded clean-input column as the 2-component vector (1, 0): the column relation (conjugate-transpose times itself) gives (1,0).(1,0) = 1, so the single active clean-input column is still a unit column orthonormal to the (absent) others. But the row relation (matrix times its own transpose on the physical register) now has rows (1,0) and (0,0): the second row is the zero vector, so the matrix-times-transpose is diag(1,0), NOT the 2-by-2 identity. Hence padding breaks 'rows orthonormal' (core*core-transpose = I fails) while keeping 'active clean-input columns orthonormal' (the column Gram matrix on active indices stays the identity). This is a general phenomenon: zero-padding adds all-zero output rows, and a matrix with a zero row can never satisfy matrix*matrix-transpose = I (that identity forces every row to have unit norm). What survives is the column isometry restricted to the active clean-input labels, because the extra padded output rows are identically zero and contribute nothing to the column inner products. The library therefore states the preserved property as orthonormality of the active clean-input columns after embedding, and uses only that; the naive 'rows stay orthonormal on the physical register' claim is false and is correctly avoided.

question: The special-orthogonal completion result guarantees that prescribed orthonormal columns can be extended to a determinant-+1 orthogonal matrix WHENEVER the number of prescribed columns is strictly less than the ambient dimension. A student conjectures the strict inequality is just a technical convenience and that the result still holds when the prescribed columns already fill all the positions (number of prescribed columns equal to the ambient dimension).
